maintopic: ASSISTANCE IN EXPORT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA AND NOVA SCOTIA APPLES-MR. HERRIDGE
ASSISTANCE IN EXPORT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA AND NOVA SCOTIA APPLES-MR. HERRIDGE
speechtext:
Just briefly I wish to bring to the attention of the house a matter of great importance to the apple growers of British Columbia and Nova Scotia, with regard to the possibility of exporting certain export varieties of apples to Great Britain this year. Some few days ago, after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had made his statement with regard to Canada giving $20,000,000 aid to relieve distressed conditions in Europe I asked him this question: In view of the fact that the British government have announced that, owing to the shortage of dollars, they will not be able to purchase apples from Canada this year, will the Canadian government give consideration to making similar arrangements for the export of certain varieties of Canadian apples to Great Britain, say in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000 worth. This proposal originated with the fruit organizations in my own constituency in British Columbia, has been widely publicized and has received support from the fruit organizations both in British Columbia and in the maritimes. It is of particular concern to growers of certain varieties of apples, particularly in British Columbia. There is the Jonathan, a small red variety which, has little sale on the Canadian domestic market, but which is purchased to a great extent in Great Britain by poor families. They like to buy a box of apples, which contains a great many of them, and give the children an apple a day before going to school. A box lasts a long time. There is a certain variety known as Cox's Orange, which is exported largely to Great Britain. There is very little sale for Cox's Orange in Canada or in the United States because the Canadian palate does not seem to be attracted bjr that variety. I understand1 that the same condition exists in Nova Scotia with regard to Graven-steins. Again I urge that consideration be given to this question.

I might say that the fruit growers of British Columbia have received hundreds of letters this year from housewives in Great Britain, expressing appreciation of the apples which have been shipped to Great Britain, since the end of the war, and how much they would like to see them again. I hope that some arrangement will be made so that the British people, particularly the poor people, may have an opportunity to purchase the varieties I have mentioned. I urge the government to give consideration to assisting the fruit growers of British Columbia and Nova Scotia in this respect. At the same time they will be assisting a great people whom we should be concerned about assisting.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
maintopic: ASSISTANCE IN EXPORT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA AND NOVA SCOTIA APPLES-MR. HERRIDGE
speechtext:
I wish to say to hon. members who have spoken in this debate that the attention of the appropriate ministers will be called to the subject matter of their remarks. The government has been deeply impressed1 with the serious situation at Dauphin, as mentioned by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews). I understand that the Brandon area is also being damaged by flood conditions. The hon. member for Dauphin was kind enough to say that the Department of Reconstruction and Supply had given highest priority to the requirements of that area for reconstruction.
I can assure him that if anything further is needed in that direction it will be forthcoming.
The attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will be called to the remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) in the matter of the interpretation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I think I know the Minister of Agriculture well enough to be able to say that if the situation comes within the orbit of the act, the act will be interpreted in as favourable manner as is possible. The hon. member mentioned work in progress by the Department of Mines and Resources. It is unfortunate that this acute flooding occurred before the results of that work could alleviate the situation, but I can assure the hon. member that the surveys which have been made will be followed up and that remedial steps will be taken so that, we hope, thd same condition cannot occur in other years.
I shall be glad to call the matter of both used and new car prices, to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), under whose jurisdiction the matter came before the removal of controls. Whether at this late stage it is possible to consider the restoration of controls in a market which was

Supply-Transport
always difficult to control, even under war conditions, I am doubtful; but in any event the minister will be informed of the remarks which have been made.
The matter of apples is receiving the urgent attention of the government, and I feel sure that a solution will be found to the conditions which have arisen as a result of a shortage of dollars in the United Kingdom.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
Air servicekkO. Air transport board, salaries and office expenses, $150,000.
I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee a situation which is greatly disturbing the good people of my little city.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just the good people?

There are no bad people; they are all very good, and the great bulk of them are very much concerned over a situation that has arisen there. I do not want to take any more of the time of the committee on this matter than is necessary, but it has to do with Donald M. Walz, a veteran with a wonderful record in the air force. He gave good service as an instructor in Canada. Then he went overseas and was shot down behind the enemy lines shortly after D-day. He was taken prisoner but escaped through his association with the underground. He came back, reported for duty and flew again until he was later shot down over Germany, where he remained a prisoner until the end of the war. He returned to Canada, where he obtained a licence as a civilian pilot, and is an excellent one by every standard on which he has been tested. Then he formed a partnership with another man by the name of Schrader, who operates a farm south of Swift Current and also a business, in both of which he is very successful. I might add that Mr. Shrader is not a veteran, not by design but because he was not accepted for service. This partnership was formed with the intention of operating an air training school and a charter air service for that part of southwestern Saskatchewan, which requires a service of that kind.
Prior to Mr. Walz being released from the air force, another gentleman, who is not a veteran but who otherwise is an excellent citizen, made application for a similar licence. Please do not misunderstand me when I compare these two men. One is a veteran with a fine service record; the other is a good citizen and a successful business man. He arrived in
Swift Current some time before Walz and Schrader came there, and both asked the air transport board for a licence to operate the same kind of service. The civilian gentleman is Mr. Karels. He operates several cold storage plants in Saskatchewan and Alberta and has other business interests which make him independent and not in need of rehabilitation measures, while Mr. Walz needs to be rehabilitated. That is the difference between the two. They both applied to the air transport board, and I have in my hand decision serial numer 211, which sets out the application of Russell E. Karels as follows:
. . . for a licence to operate the following commercial air services from a base at Swift Current, Saskatchewan: non-scheduled charter to transport passengers and goods, flying training and recreational flying (sightseeing and barnstorming) .
In his case the application was approved. The other application is described as follows:
Application by Donald II. Walz and Charles W. Schrader, carrying on business under the firm name and style of Swift Current Air Services, for a licence to operate the following commercial air services from a base at Swift Current, Saskatchewan: non-scheduled charter to transport passengers and goods, flying training and recreational flying (sightseeing and barnstorming).
Decision: application denied.
I take exception to the denial of this licence, particularly on the grounds set out by the examiner for the air transport board, who stated that Karels had a substantial investment in local business and a permanent residence in Swift Current. He also had his application in slightly before the other application, and his financial statement shows assets in the air service of over $28,000, including a capital investment of $25,000, with $40,000 in cold storage plants at Swift Current and elsewhere and substantial interests in Calgary, Lethbridge and Humboldt. Apparently it was considered that because of his financial position he was more likely to be a successful operator of an air service. I should like to point out to>
the minister that Swift Current Air Services, comprising Walz and Schrader, have assets of $12,000, of which $10,000 have already been subscribed, and that the partners have additional assets of $30,900, consisting of bonds, grain, farm machinery, land and sundry assets which could be easily liquidated, and which would furnish sufficient capital for their purposes.
The air transport board sent a gentleman to hold hearings and decide the issue. The hearings were held, and I have in my hand a complete verbatim transcript of the proceedings. I am not going to take time to put it on the record, but it indicates that the reasons I
Supply-Transport

have cited as those given by the examining officer are correct; that is, it was felt that Karels had a prior claim because his application had -been made first and also because he was in a slightly better financial position. I believe the decision should have been the other way, because the veteran and his partner had sufficient assets and certainly needed rehabilitation more than the well-off gentleman.
I am not alone in this view. I have had frequent representations from the Canadian Legion there, and there have been items in the local weekly newspaper, which is one of the best in Canada, having frequently won the prize in that field. Even the board of trade, while it did not make any particular recommendation, threw the balance of its support in favour of Walz and Schrader on the ground that Walz is a veteran with an excellent record, and that the partners have sufficient capital and knowledge to go ahead with the project. I have also letters from other branches of the Canadian Legion and others supporting the case of the veteran, but I do not think it is necessary to take time to put them on the record. They are available to anyone who wishes to look at them, and I am trying to make a fair presentation of the case. I am not saying anything that cannot be supported by documentary evidence, and the file on this matter is quite lengthy. If I may, however, I should 'ike to read a resolution on this matter by the board of trade, which appeared in the Sun, :he newspaper I mentioned a moment ago:
At a general meeting of the board of trade in the Healy hotel on Tuesday evening, a resolution was unanimously adopted in connection with the recent announcement that in the granting of a commercial air service licence, a veteran, Don Walz, had been denied a licence, one of the reasons being given that one service is all that is economically feasible for Swift -Current.
The meeting went on record as disapproving this action of the examining officer who later made his recommendations to the air transport board at Ottawa. In addition the meeting felt that a returned veteran should have been given equal consideration when he was trying to reestablish himself and apparently had been led to believe that his application would get favourable consideration. The resolution will be directed to the proper authorities at Ottawa. President Slater Alexander presided at the meeting.
Mr. Slater Alexander is a fine gentleman. I should like to draw attention to another factor that entered into this examination. When any person makes an application to the air transport board for a licence to operate a service anyone who feels that that person is not the proper type can make representations to the board and oppose the application. Mr. Karels made representations which are to be found in the transcript of evidence.

He opposed the granting of a licence to Walz and Schrader, the veterans concerned. His opposition was on the ground that there was not room for two services in the area.
On the other hand, the evidence showed that Mr. Walz and Mr. Schrader were prepared to compete for the field. They were willing to spend what money they had in- the belief that they could give the kind of service which would either make them paramount in the field of competition or establish the fact that there was room for two services. They made no representations opposing the application of Mr. Karels. This should be distinctly in favour of Walz and Schrader when the matter is being considered by anyone who believes in the right of free competition, as many in this committee do. Walz and Schrader were not asking any favours; they were willing to let Karels operate, provided that they could operate. They contended that if there were room for two they would both be able to exist; if there were not, the best man would win. I understand that to be competition. They were willing to adopt that attitude, -but Mr. Karels was not. He opposed the veteran and his partner getting a licence.
I have another clipping from the Sun dealing with the same matter, and if the minister and the committee want it placed on the record I shall do so, although it is fairly long. It simply supports the statement I have already made. I do not wish to delay the deliberations of the committee, but I did want to place this matter squarely before the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply who administers the air transport board and to plead with him to see that the government do what they have said they are going to do, give the veteran every opportunity to rehabilitate himself.
As I said before, anyone reading the evidence will arrive at the same conclusion, that the veteran and his partner are qualified by every test that could be made. These men have the ability and the means and the knowledge of business administration to operate this service. They are willing to compete and they ask for a charter. On the other hand, the other man wants to exclude them from that field in order to have it for himself. While I do not think he is a wealthy man, he is well enough established in other lines of business not to require rehabilitation. He can get along quite comfortably without his air operations.
I should like the minister to give the committee and myself, and particularly the people back home who are so concerned with this, some assurance that he will take a personal interest in this case. I believe if he does he

Supply-Transport
will have no hesitation in saying that this veteran flyer has at least as good a right if not a greater right to this charter. I say all this without any criticism or charge against the examining officer. I expect that he had certain terms of reference and probably he did what he thought was best. However I disagree with his finding, and I want to impress the minister with my reasons for disagreement. If the minister cannot make a statement now I ask him to assure us that he will give personal consideration to this matter which is so deserving.

I want to thank the hon. member for Swift Current for placing this matter before the committee in some detail. I am quite familiar with the case, as it was called to my attention some days ago. I have read the evidence and looked into the matter thoroughly. There were two applicants for the same licence. The function of the air transport board is to rehabilitate the veteran in a manner which will permit him to make a living, not in a manner which may get him into difficulties where he may lose his gratuity and other assets. That is the reason why some care is taken in sorting out applicants for licences of the type in question.
As I say, there were two applications. Karels' application was the prior one, the application of Walz and Schrader coming in at a later date. The examiner -was sent to Swift Current to investigate. A hearing -was held and written evidence was taken. The recommendation of the examiner was followed in issuing a licence to Karels. My understanding of the situation is that Karels is a resident of Swift Current, whereas the veteran Walz has never been a resident there.

Karels had not been a resident for long. He came in there only recently; I think he was there for less than a year when he made his application.
Mr. HOWrE: It was thought by the board that there were other desirable locations as a centre for flying and that possibly the veteran Walz could locate in an area which might provide a better living. Representations were made by the board of trade and responsible citizens of Swift Current suggesting that licences should be issued to both parties. Personally I am reluctant to accept them because I think eventually one of the licensees will lose his investment, but who am I not to bow to local opinion? There is no great principle at stake. The air transport board is holding hearings in the west at the present time, and I have asked the board to stop at Swift Current and hold another hearing so as to
ascertain whether there is any serious reason why both applications should not be granted. I am inclined to think the result will be that both applicants will be granted a licence. I hope my hon. friend will not be reluctant in taking his share of the responsibility in case the situation ends in disaster.

I will not. I thank the minister very much.
Mr. 'WINTERS: Under what items will the T.C.A. be considered?
Mr! HOWE: The T.C.A., being a selfsupporting enterprise, has no estimate. It earns its own revenue and does not depend on parliament for funds.
From the report I had, I thought there was a deficit.
It had an earlier surplus to cover the deficit. I shall be glad to have my hon. friend discuss the T.C.A. under this item if he cares to.

I should like to say a few words in connection with what seems to be a growing complaint about T.C.A. service in the maritimes. Almost everyone who flies to Ottawa comes to see me to complain about what they say is an increasingly badl service to the maritimes, a service which I had always thought was increasingly good. They complain of long stop-overs in Montreal which make it necessary for people to leave here in the middle of the night, wait in Montreal, leave Montreal still later in the morning and then arrive in Halifax on the same day. They complain of the lengthy stop-overs.
Another serious cause for complaint is the uncertainty as to when the planes will leave both from Halifax and from Montreal. I hear an increasing number of complaints from people who have called up the air port to find out what time the plane is leaving; when they get to the field they find the departure has been delayed for an hour or two, and they come back to town and then find still further delays. During the past week or so, an eminent gentleman from the maritimes took off from Halifax and the plane made an unscheduled stop at Blissville. There were ladies on the plane, and at Blissville there were no facilities whatsoever for ladies or anybody else.
I have stopped at Blissville several times. I hope my hon. friend has.

I was told that the facilities had been removed from the buildings. It was a hot day and the place was almost insufferable because of mosquitoes. In the Light of all these complaints I should be
Supply-Transport

pleased to hear the minister make a statement, because I know there must be something to be said on the other side too, on the service to the maritimes.

I am surprised to hear my hon. friend speak of a lack of service to the maritimes, as operating results indicate that T.C.A. may be giving them too much service. T.C.A. has four flights daily from Montreal to Halifax and these are running about fifty per cent occupancy, whereas in the very busy section, Montreal-Ottawa, Toronto-Winnipeg, there are four flights, all running nearly 100 per cent occupancy, with many complaints because of lack of accommodation. The same care is taken in operating T.C.A. in the maritimes as elsewhere on the system. I would not mention the peculiar weather conditions on that route at a time like this, but sometimes we do have difficulty at the Halifax end, and sometimes difficulty at Pennfield. The only reason for going to Blissville was that Pennfield was closed in on that particular day. Blissville is not a regular stop at the present time. Pennfield is a well-equipped air port and ordinarily that is the stop. I can assure my hon, friend that, so far as weather in all parts of Canada is concerned, we have had the worst four months that have ever been experienced on our air lines. I think he will find that the operation is sound, and that, with the improved weather that we always get in summer and autumn in the maritimes, we shall have first-class operation.
Would it not be possible to arrange a schedule from Ottawa to Halifax to avoid the lay-over in Montreal and work out a better through service?

There are four services daily, but perhaps my hon. friend takes the evening plane. That plane is held to meet the convenience of the Post Office Department, to collect the last mail from Montreal. If my hon. friend would take one of the earlier services he could make better connections.

Would the minister give us a short statement with regard to the domestic aviation situation and the policy of the government at the present time, also with regard to the international aviation picture. For example, I understand that it has not been possible to work out any multilateral agreement, which was the original policy announced by the government several years ago. I think it would be helpful if the minister would give us a short statement with regard to both the domestic and the international aviation situation.

I was going to ask the minister much the same question. Would he include

in his statement a comparison of how T.C.A. has survived the last six or eight months, which have been so difficult for the United States air lines, and has he any views to offer on our organization as compared with theirs?

In the international field, as hon. members are aware, PICAO, the international civil aviation organization, has Canada as its location and Montreal as its headquarters. That orgnization has been meeting continuously since its formation, and at its last assembly, in May of this year, it became a permanent organization, with its headquarters at Montreal. The location of the international organization in that city has been helpful to Canadian aviation, and has helped to place Canada prominently on the world air maps.
The international organization has been dealing with the matter of a multilateral agreement. An attempt has been made to arrive at common ground, but to date that attempt has not been successful. The last meeting of the international organization debated the subject at great length, but failed to reach agreement and decided that a special meeting of the organization would be called for this autumn in Rio de Janeiro for the sole purpose of discussing the problem of a multilateral agreement. Therefore I can report at the present time that there is no multilateral agreement covering traffic matters other than the first two freedoms; that is, the freedom to fly over a country for peaceful purposes and the freedom to land for repairs or refueling. The first and second freedoms are the only multilateral freedoms at present. In the meantime, a great many bilateral agreements have been made. Canada has made five or six, all of which have been reported to this House of Commons. To date we have not given the fifth freedom, as have some other countries. We believe our location is such that our agreement should be confined to the first four freedoms. We have kept to that course.
Would the minister explain the third, fourth and fifth freedoms?

The first freedom is the right to fly over a country for peaceful purposes. The second freedom is the right to land for repairs or refueling. The third freedom is the right to pick up passengers in the home country and take them to any other country with which Canada has a fourth freedom agreement. The fourth freedom is the right to pick up passengers in any country in which Canada has traffic rights and bring those passengers to the home country. The fifth freedom is the right of a Canadian air line to pick up passengers, we will say, in the United

Supply-Transport
Kingdom and deliver them in France. It is the right to handle passengers who are not nationals of its own country or destined to or from its own country.
We are not prepared to give that freedom?

We have not as yet. We are prepared to give it on a multilateral basis. If there is a universal exchange of fifth freedom rights we are prepared to join, but our situation on the air lines is such that we feel that bilateral agreements granting fifth freedom rights would work to our detriment so far as Canadian traffic is concerned.
On the international routes at the present time we are operating eleven round-trip crossings a week between Montreal, Prestwick, Scotland, and London, England. The flights are running full at the moment, We are operating the new North Star planes. These planes have worked out amazingly well. I think no other new aircraft has taken the punishment in its initial operations that the North Star has been subjected to. With five planes in commission, we have been operating eleven round trips a week across the Atlantic, which is rather a phenomenal operation. In some cases the turn-around time at London is no longer than an hour and a quarter. The plane delivers its passengers there, takes its load and returns to Canada with no more overhaul than can be performed in that time.
What is the length of time taken in crossing over each way?
The schedule is fourteen hours from Montreal to London, with an intermediate stop at Prestwick.
Can the minister say whether the United States firm which operates out of Montreal cuts into the T.C.A. business at all?
What United States firm is that?
I saw an advertisement in the paper in which a United States firm was advertising flights to England.
That would not be the Ontario government immigration project?
No, from Montreal.
Acting in competition with you.

The Ontario government immigration plan has made arrangements with a United States charter operator, I believe, to bring their immigrants from the United Kingdom to Canada, but there may be some difficulty about working out details of the operation.
This was an advertisement in the Montreal Star advertising flights to England. I do not know whether they go via New York or not.
They must be advertising a flight from some point outside Canada which can be reached by a connecting line.
Do you not need more than five aircraft?

We have twenty on the way. As my hon. friend knows, we are using an interim aircraft now. We took five of the twenty aircraft being built for the R.C.A.F. As a matter of fact, we are using these until the pressurized version is completed, the first of which will be out this month. By late autumn we expect to have twenty pressurized aircraft, which will represent the permanent international planes for T.C.A. As far as the domestic services are concerned, they have been expanded. In the maritimes we are operating four services a day between Montreal and Halifax; two of them go on to Sydney and Newfoundland. We also have a new service operating between Halifax, Yarmouth, Pennfield in New Brunswick, and Boston; two services each day. In the central region service is about as last reported. From Winnipeg west there have been some changes. We have opened a, new route, Winnipeg to Edmonton by way of Saskatoon, a direct route. We have opened a new route between Winnipeg and Calgary direct, and we have put on a service from Winnipeg to Lethbridge, with stops at Swift Current and Medicine Hat, These are the new developments in the field.
When are you flying across the great lakes?
We are flying across the great lakes at the present time. All flights from Toronto to Winnipeg are across the great lakes, with stops at Sault Ste. Marie, Port Arthur and Winnipeg.
What time is cut off by crossing the great lakes?
As I remember it, about an hour and fifteen minutes.

What is the main obstacle to the completion of a multilateral agreement? Is the United States against a multilateral agreement at the present time? Originally that nation was very much in favour of a multilateral agreement. What are the main obstacles to the completion, of such an agreement?

The main obstacles to a multilateral agreement are that the various
Supply-Transport

countries believe that there should be limitations to competition, and limitation on the number of services. There are various differing opinions which I think can, in time,, be reconciled. Discussions seem to be coming more in the direction of reconciliation, and I am quite hopeful that the conference in Rio this autumn will bring about agreement. The reason there is no multilateral agreement. today is that the countries have not been able to reach a sufficient measure of agreement to make it possible.
What position does the United States take?

That country has its own idea of what an agreement should be, which differs from ours and differs from that of the United Kingdom, and differs from that of many countries. In the last assembly, the Canadian proposals seemed to have the support of the smaller countries, but they did not have the support of the United States or of the United Kingdom.

When is it expected that the . transpacific flights will be started? I believe the Australians are now giving that service, and New Zealand is also doing so. When will Canada have a service to Australia and New Zealand?

The present service is being operated under the sponsorship of Australia, New Zealand and1 the United Kingdom which share the expenses. It is actually being operated by a private company in Australia, Australian Airways. The undertaking was that Canada would run a parallel service as soon as we could make the necessary arrangements, and that still holds. Just when it will be I cannot say at the moment. We had never expected to be running eleven round trips a week across the Atlantic. I think we could put twice that number of trips on and still be booked full in both directions. Faced with that situation, we are at the moment, reluctant to divert planes from that service. With more planes coming out this autumn, I hope that early next year we shall be able to undertake the Pacific service as well as the service through the West Indies to South America.

Are there any penalty clauses in the agreement to take delivery of these machines from Canadair because it definitely penalizes the T.C.A. in its further expansion to be held up for months and months in getting delivery of aircraft? As I understand it, the first machines to come off the line were RjC.A.F. machines. They are just a temporary measure, and if competition is very

keen in this field and the T.C.A. is to keep up its good reputation, then an assured supply of planes on schedule is absolutely necessary to its continued operation.

Trans-Canada Air Lines could have borrowed more of the military type planes except that the cost of converting them into luxury passenger planes and converting them back to military planes is an item that should not be enlarged too greatly. There has been no particular hold-up. The only hold-up has been the slow delivery o-f Rolls-Royce engines, which resulted from the blackout in industry in the United Kingdom last winter. I understand that deliveries are now improving. I understand, that ten or a dozen of the military type planes are ready for delivery, except for engines. The arrangement was that the military type of plane would be finished first, and the pressurized type, which has a good many differences in structure, would follow. The schedule for the first pressurized type plane was always July. It is my understanding that there will be no delay in delivering the twenty pressurized planes to the T.C.A. on schedule set up in the contract.

Has the minister investigated the possibility of having a good aircraft engine made in Canada or a Canadian contract to make the Rolls-Royce engines here? The ridiculous part of this whole business is having an American boat company manufacture an American hull with a British engine in the Dominion of Canada. Our air picture is just as ridiculous as that.
My hon. friend has his own idea of what is ridiculous.
I say that is.

This whole production was Canadian sponsored. The original design was turned out by Canadian engineers and the original production was carried out by Canadians. It is only the fact that the government. felt it should not properly be in the business of manufacturing and selling aircraft that induced it to sell to a company which, though certainly it has United States capital, contains on its board of directors a number of able Canadian business men. It is no more a United States company than a good many others that I could name which are respectable Canadian companies as far as ownership goes. We believe that Electric Boat had a type of experience that was valuable to the operations. It is not a United States plane. It is true we have a basic design from the United States, but Douglas would be the last to say that they care to sponsor a design that is flying the

Supply-Transport
Atlantic in the name of the North Star today. It is a Canadian version of what is required for the route, based on Douglas design. The Rolls-Royce was chosen, first, because it is of British make. It did not represent a drain on Canadian dollars, and we believed it was the engine most suitable for aircraft to perform the service we had in mind in the North Star planes.

I am aware of all these things, but you cannot control operations properly nor can you control production if you cannot get parts in Canada. You should set out to have every part you can make in that aircraft produced in Canada, employing Canadian labour and industry.

The immediate requirements for Rolls-Royce engines would be perhaps 160 or 170 or 200. The cost of setting up an establishment to build them would be in the neighbourhood of $15 million or $20 million. The cost per engine would be colossal. I was criticized by hon. members opposite for what they thought would be the cost of the North Star planes. That they were mistaken about that cost does not mean that they would not be. fully justified in condemning such a capital cost for so small a production of engines. We must use reason in these things. I admit at once the desirability of the objective. I wish we made Rolls-Royce engines in Canada, but I would not recommend to parliament appropriations of the size necessary to bring that about.

Did the minister not explore
this matter during the war? He spent $21,825,777.33 on Cartierville. The sum of $15 million more spent during the war to produce a good engine in Canada would have been money well spent in a post-war programme.

During the war we spent $21
million on Cartierville and we had a production in excess of $100 million worth of equipment over the years. If I could spend another $15 million and turn out $60 million worth of engine equipment I would be happy to recommend the expenditure.

Probably the mistake was
made during the war.

I should like to ask the minister a question in reference to the air service in the maritime provinces. What principle governs the schedule by which these planes fly? It seems to me that they are not getting as great a popular support as they should, and I was wondering to what extent the flights were used for passenger and mail service respectively. Going east from Ottawa,
there are two flights a day. One takes place at an opportune time in the morning but the other comes at midnight. If one is going to Moncton and from there on to the island, one has to fly at an uncomfortable hour and can get no sleep. The passenger arrives around five-thirty or six-thirty o'clock in the morning. There is another flight that could be made in the morning if you could get to Montreal to catch the six-thirty o'clock plane. If there were some other hour at which these planes flew there might be a more popular use of them. I am wondering whether the schedules have been drawn up from the point of view of passengers or with the mail service in view.

On all routes we must have
one mail service. There is one plane that serves the convenience of the Post Office Department and that plane is never very convenient to passengers. It must not be forgotten that we get considerable revenue from the post office. The schedules are balanced to meet connecting planes, having in mind the desirability of choosing hours that are of the greatest convenience to the travelling public.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Although this has been
said before, I feel that this item should not pass without a word of commendation to the minister for the service and the courtesy and safety being afforded in the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines. Those who have travelled by air can appreciate the point of view expressed by an hon. member to the effect that it is a bit annoying sometimes to have to wait for a take-off, but most of us who have had that experience realize that it is a guarantee of safety so far as the operations of the air lines are concerned. The experience that has been had in some other countries in recent months during some bad weather we have been having simply serves to highlight the splendid record that our Canadian air line has achieved, and we are all extremely proud of it.
I think, too, a word should be said, not only for this record of safety, but for the service which Trans-Canada Air Lines is rendering to this country, and which may not be fully recognized until historians of tthe future write about this period. It is serving to unite the country, and in every way, it seems to me, this is one achievement that the minister can speak of with a great deal of pride. On the other hand, there are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister about another phase of the work of the air transport board, or indeed about another phase of civil aviation policy. I would ask the minister whether
Supply-Transport

the government or the air transport board is giving any consideration to an over-all plan with respect to Canada's north land. The minister knows the disagreements I have with him over the policy he is pursuing with respect to the north land, but at the moment I will confine myself to a few questions.
I take the position that we have, to the north in this country, a continent in itself, rich in minerals, oil and other natural resources, and the fact that we have that country up there places certain responsibilities upon us. We should be thinking in terms of its fullest development, both for its own sake, for the sake of Canada and for the sake of the world at large.
I recall remarks that the minister has made in the past about mistakes that were made in the early days of railroading. I hope that similar mistakes are not now being made in the early days of civil aviation. I do not like the idea of that north country seeming, as it does to me, to be just a field for exploitation by private companies in the direction of transportation on the one hand, and mining on the other, particularly when these companies are interwoven as they are.
We have up there minerals and oil in a great expanse of country, and I think that in the process of developing new plans for that country we should be looking, not just in the direction of private exploitation, but in the direction of what is best for that country for the sake of Canada and for the benefit of the world at large. I should like to know from the minister whether the air transport board is just receiving such applications as come along from Canadian Pacific Air Lines and others, considering them and granting them; or whether any over-all planning is being done with respect to the northern half of this country, particularly in relation to air service.

I may say that the most careful planning of the northern services has been and is being carried out by the air transport board. One of the first acts of the board was to travel over every existing route and service in Canada. The requirements of each area were investigated. The service being given was explored and the needs for further service were noted. I might point out to hon. members that a tremendous expansion in aviation has taken place from 1939 to the end of 1946. The personnel engaged in the air services has been multiplied approximately by ten; the miles flown have been multiplied by more than six, and the areas served have been greatly increased. Before the war there was a great deal of dissatisfaction with the service given in certain areas, and among. those

engaged in air transport work there was a good deal of dissatisfaction with regard to unfair and cut-throat competition. Both complaints have pretty well disappeared. I know of no area today which has more than an occasional complaint about the service being rendered by air transport.
I was happy to look over the operating results for 1946 of all the air operators in Canada. I may say that one service which the air transport board has rendered is the establishment of a statistical department which gives prompt and accurate statistics of the industry as a whole. A study of those results for 1946 indicates that, with amazingly few exceptions, the operation of air services had been profitable to the operators. A great number of new services have been undertaken by retruned men. It has been the business of the board to try to place these veterans in areas where they could make a satisfactory living; and that objective has been attained beyond my greatest expectations. Occasionally we are told that in carrying out that objective we are being unfair to someone. The hon. member for Swift Current suggests that we are being unfair to a veteran in his city. My own thought was that the difficulty arose because we were trying to be fair to the veteran. We were trying to tell him that he would find a better field in some other part of western Canada. However we cannot carry these points too far. If the veteran feels we are doing him a wrong, we will right the wrong, and let his own judgment prevail. Perhaps we were wrong. But in general we have succeeded in convincing new operators that they would be wise not to enter the territory they had in mind in the first instance. We have been able to show them the potential traffic in the area. Careful traffic studies have been made of every part of Canada. When a veteran or pioneer in aviation comes to the air transport board and talks about an area, the board is able to produce a traffic study of the area and tell him what they believe to be the potential traffic of the area and give him advice as to whether or not he is wise to undertake to make an investment and try to make his living from that particular area. I believe the air transport board has performed a great service for aviation in sorting out th'e industry, in making sure that the user of the service has service, and in making sure that operators in the service are given a fair competitive position.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Will the minister indicate the proportion in the northern services, say on the route to Yellowknife and the routes down in the Mackenzie? What is the proportion as between Canadian Pacific Air Lines

Supply-Transport
on the one hand and these smaller services operated by veterans on the other? Will the minister also tell us if Canadian Pacific Air Lines is now showing a profit on these northern operations?

I cannot give an arbitrary proportion. In general, a preview of the routes by the air transport board resulted in the Canadian Pacific Air Lines retaining the routes that could be operated on wheels with heavy equipment. They kept the route from Edmonton over the northwest staging route to Alaska. They kept the service to Yellowknife. They gave up a great variety of services which were formerly operated on floats and skis; and those services, generally speaking, were assigned to newcomers in the field.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does anyone else operate on those main lines?
No. Similarly, we do not allow anyone else to operate on routes which we assign to operators of floats and skis, if it is a scheduled operation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What about profits?
Mr. MaoNICOL: Does the minister mean that some other operator now flies the plane from Norman Welle to Aklavik?
I am not sure.
I went on a Canadian Pacific plane.
I am not sure who operates that particular service. I shall be glad to look it up. As I remember it, that is a seaplane operation. I think it is flown by others.
It is a float plane from Norman Wells to Aklavik. I went by Canadian Pacific plane; at least, I thought so.

Yes. But that was a year or two ago. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked about profits. Canadian Pacific Air Lines showed a small profit last year, the first year of operation when Canadian Pacific Air Lines have shown a profit.

Has the minister available here comparable figures on the incidence of fatal accidents? He may or may not have those figures with him. In the case of fatal accidents and claims being made, does Trans-Canada Air Lines carry its own insurance, or does it reinsure through some other company? How are the claims settled?

I do not know that I can give just the figures on fatal accidents which my hon. friend wanted. The airways have the best record of any form of transportation with regard to number of fatalities for the
number of miles travelled. Their record is much better than that of the railroads, and much better than that of the highways. In its history T.C.A. has had two accidents in which passengers have been lost. The first occurred at Armstrong, Ontario, I think in 1941; the second tragic accident occurred this year, when a plane flying from Lethbridge to Vancouver was presumably lost in the Pacific ocean off Vancouver. At the present time T.C.A. carries its own insurance funds, and claims are settled promptly. In the early days it was customary to reinsure part of the liability, but the fund is now strong enough so that T.C.A. carries its own risk.
The figures I had in mind were those giving comparisons with other air services in the United States, not ground services. If the minister has the record it might be well to put it on Hansard.

Our safety record still stands high among the air lines of the world. We were almost perfect until the accident this spring, but it is difficult to make comparisons, as some of the smaller operations have never had an accident. Among the transcontinental operations, I think T.C.A. is easily the best.

I want to ask the minister a question in regard to the West Indies service, particularly the service to Bermuda. I understand that there was some disagreement or difficulty in getting an agreement with the authorities at Bermuda, whom I understand to be the United States army which operates the airfield there. Can the minister say what the difficulties have been, and whether any progress has been made in overcoming them. Will he also say whether it is the intention to operate an air service from Canada to the West Indies. I have one or two other questions, but this is the main one, if I can get an answer to it.

Canada has been ready and anxious to operate a service to Bermuda since December, 1945. The difficulty has been that the airport in Bermuda is one of the American bases built in British territory. The Americans were reluctant to allow other countries to use the base until an over-all agreement could be reached between the United Kingdom and some of her colonies and the United States covering the operation of all those bases. I understand that the agreement is now complete in all particulars except in regard to the use of Gander airport at Newfoundland. We have reason to be hopeful that within the next two weeks that difficulty will be overcome and the agreement in regard to the bases signed. It is the present
Supply-Transport

intention to start the service to Bermuda not later than September 1 of this year.

What other bases would come under the general agreement? The minister mentioned Gander and Bermuda. I understand that there are United States air bases on other Caribbean and West Indies islands. Is it the intention to continue the service further south than Bermuda?
'Mr. HOWE: It is our intention to continue farther south. We have agreements with Bermuda, Jamaica and Trinidad. Negotiations are continuing with Nassau, but no agreement has been reached; and it is our hope to extend the service beyond Trinidad toward Rio and perhaps farther into Latin America.

I am very glad to hear that statement.
I have just one other question in regard to the North Star. This question was asked me by several people who have been in the R.A.F. on the technical side. I understand that the North Star is using the Merlin engine. Is that a specially designed engine for peacetime use? It is not the war type of Merlin engine?

At the beginning of the mail operation with the Lancasters we attempted to use military type engines, with indifferent success. Modifications were brought about and a satisfactory engine was developed for that operation. The Merlin engines at present in use are a complete modification even of the engines used in the Lancasters. It is a highly developed engine with special characteristics for transport work, and I am happy to say that we are very well satisfied with the results of our operation.

One more question and I am through. I am not a member of the railway committee, but hon. gentlemen who are on that committee said they thought some of this information was given there. Is there available a break-down showing the amount of freight carried on lines other than T.CA.? Does the air transport board keep a record of the ton-miles of freight and the passenger-miles of other services? I know T.C.A. has such a record, but is there also a record in connection with C.P.A. and the other smaller air lines that are licensed at the present time?

We have complete data on the freight carried on each separate route. That information is contained in the annual report of the air transport board. It is also contained in monthly bulletins that are issued. If my hon. friend is interested I shall be glad to send him the information.
Thank you very much.

A few moments ago the minister refered to the loss of a trans-Canada air liner off the coast of British Columbia last April. Is he in a position to give the committee the result of the inquiry into the loss of that plane? Some time ago I asked the minister whether a board of inquiry would be set up, and at that time he indicated this would be done. Since then I have not heard the results of that inquiry.

A board of inquiry was immediately established and a thorough investigation was carried out. The operation was checked from every possible angle, and no flaw could be found in the operation or the condition of the plane. The report of the board was published. It boiled down to this, that for no known reason the plane disappeared in the few minutes between its passage over the airport and its usual landing time. It reported in over the airport. Ten minutes later an attempt was made to reach it by radio, when it had not landed on schedule, but the attempt to make radio contact failed, and no trace of the plane was found thereafter. The consensus of all concerned seems to be that something occurred over the Pacific, and that the plane is at the bottom of the ocean.
Is that evidence available to members of the house?
Yes.

I feel obligated to congratulate the minister on having maintained the Canadian Pacific air service in the northwestern part of Canada. I remember that when the bill was going through the house I vigorously opposed one proposal, but I am now very glad to congratulate the minister on having maintained that service. I have nothing but confidence in what is done by T.C.A.; as one other hon. member has said, it gives a splendid service, and its personnel are of the best. Since no one has spoken about the Canadian Pacific service, however, I am going to do so because they do render a splendid service in that north country. Everyone who travels on their planes speaks just as highly of the personnel of Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and of their courtesy to travellers, as we all speak of T.C.A. In my judgment Canada is well served by both these lines, and I hope the minister will maintain them both. He really fathered the T.C.A., and I hope he will continue to maintain Canadian Pacific Air Lines up in northwestern Canada. They are a private concern and are doing an excellent

Supply-Transport
job in opening up that part of the country. I wish them every success.
What is delaying the arrangements to fly the Pacific from Vancouver to Australia and New Zealand?

No particular delay, except that all the planes that we have immediately available are working on more profitable routes. When we get more equipment and trained crews we expect to undertake the Pacific run.
A year ago the Canadian ambassador to Mexico announced that the T.C.A. was to fly from Canada to Mexico City, while a Mexican line would fly to Canada. Has that proposal been dropped?

I think the announcement was that a Mexican line intended to fly from Mexico to Canada. Canada has never entertained a proposal to fly a service to Mexico City. No bilateral agreement has been signed between Mexico and Canada. There were discussions, but I understand they were dropped. I think the enthusiasm in Mexico City died down.

In 1945 an amendment to the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act was passed, by which power was given to set up crown companies under Trans-Canada Air Lines. Have any such companies been set up and, if so, what are they?
Trans-Canada Atlantic Air Lines is operating the north Altantic service.
Is that the only one?
Yes.
When does T.CjA. plan to inaugurate flights to Sweden to implement the joint agreement that was signed?

T.C.A. has no' present plans for operating a service from Canada to Sweden. We have the right to do so, but we know of no Canadian traffic between Canada and Sweden which -would warrant a service between the two countries.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Could the minister say something with regard to the private plane situation in Canada, the personal plane or the so-called flivver plane? Is any encouragement being given to the development of this kind of flying? What is the situation at the present time in Canada, as compared with that in the United States?

Every encouragement short of subsidy 'has been given. We subsidized flying schools to teach our citizens to fly in private
planes. We have worked out a system of charges at air ports which allows the small private plane to land without paying a landing fee. We have put in a scale of hangar rentals which permits the small plane to have accommodation at a lower cost than the large planes. We have made the air as free as possible to the private plane. As far as I know, anyone who desires to fly privately in Canada can have a very good time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the minister any figures of the number of private planes in Canada and in the United States? When he gives that answer, would he answer a question on the other side of the picture? What is the situation with regard to safety precautions in connection with private flying?
The annual report of the department dated March 31, 1946, indicated that there were twenty-seven private aircraft licensed in Canada and 446 commercial aircraft as of that date.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the minister the figure for the United States?

No. The enthusiasm for private flying is not as great today as it was before the war. Commercial air lines services have been developed to a great extent since the war. It is much safer for a man who may wish to travel from point to point to go by the commercial air lines. Fifteen or twenty years ago I used to be very fond of flying about in anyone's private plane, but today I would not step into a private plane if I could avoid doing so. I prefer to travel on the air lines. I have had an opportunity of seeing the safety measures taken by the air lines, both in the air and on the ground, as well as the communications services and so on, which are not available to the private aeroplane. All I can say is that, if anybody wishes to fly a plane himself, he has my blessing, but I take no responsibility.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I agree wholly with the minister. I was just asking for information.
Many of those planes would be company-owned planes used in company operations?
No.. The planes my hon. friend speaks of would be listed as commercial planes. They would be owned and operated by companies.

I wish to echo much of what has been said about the service given by T.C.A. I have, however, a complaint to make which, while it is of a somewhat personal nature, will, I believe, be regarded as being reasonable. I
Supply-Transport

wish the seats could be placed farther apart. I think I will get support in this from the Minister of Fisheries. This would add greatly to my comfort and I hope the minister will take it into consideration.

If the hon. member will patronize our North Star trans-Atlantic service he will find that we have put in only thirty-six seats in the space in which other competing air lines put forty-four seats. We hope that passengers of greater stature even than my hon. friend will find plenty of leg-room in the Atlantic crossing. I recommend the trip to him and I assure him that he will find it most comfortable.
I wish I could count on the minister complying with all my requests so quickly.

When planes arrive in
Canada from Great Britain or the United States Canadians are not allowed to pass through customs and immigration, first. I know at LaGuardia and other fields in the United States, United States citizens are permitted to go through customs and immigration first.

Several conferences have been held with customs and immigration officials in various countries. We are attempting to minimize the red tape now involved, in a passenger from one country arriving in another country. No one resents more deeply than I being treated as an immigrant when entering the United States, but that happens to me and. to every Canadian. The citizens of that country are taken first. We in Canada do not do that; we take them as they come. I think ours is the better method because we save the resentment which I always feel toward the other procedure.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at seven o'clock. SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT Air service-
HO. Air transport board-salaries and office expenses, $150,000.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that in the maritimes we have the Maritime Central Air-
IMr. Macdonnell.]
ways servicing Prince Edward Island and part of the maritimes, connecting up with the T.C.A. at Moncton. One little disadvantage we have is in getting reservations through Charlottetown via Moncton to go to Montreal and such places. We have always felt that we should have a few seats reserved on each plane up until at least a few hours before it leaves Moncton. If we could have those seats it would be a great help to maritime travellers and to maritime airways.
The minister knows that the president of T.C.A. made a statement in the committee on several occasions that Maritime Central Airways was one of the best feeder lines that the T.C.A. had. If the minister would look into that little matter about which the people are complaining once in a while, I am sure that it would meet with their approval and perhaps he could adjust it.

Perhaps I can say just a word. Maritime Central Airways is giving a fine service, not only to Prince Edward Island, but to such places as Pictou and the northern shore of Nova Scotia. It would be the intention of T.C.A. to give it the best of connecting service. I shall be glad to call the attention of the officials to the remarks made by my hon. friend. If any steps can be taken to improve the connection, I am sure they will be taken.

Before six o'clock we had a fairly thorough discussion of the operations of T.C.A. and of some of the air policies in Canada. We could almost call it a probe. I should like to say a few words about it generally. I do not wish anything that I have to say to be construed as criticism of the Trans-Canada Air Lines because I think, under the circumstances and perhaps even under the direction in some cases, they have done an amazing job. As an airman, I would be the first to appreciate what they have done in carrying out their schedule of eleven return flights to England with the small number of aircraft they have.
However we have been informed that they are operating with six aircraft which were destined for the R.C.A.F.; that they are unable to operate their Pacific route; that they do not plan to operate to Sweden, and that they are in need of both aircraft and crews. To me that seems like a condemnation of the policy of the government which, in this competitive age, has led them into the position where they find themselves short of engines, short of crews and1 short of aircraft. It seems to me, that the government have a job of explaining to do, because, in competitive air line travel, the fact that

Supply-Transport
Canada should be placed in this position is quite deplorable. They had the aircraft. They had the aircraft in the United Kingdom the end of the war. They had lots of Lancasters with which to fly the north Atlantic to Sweden and to the West Indies if they chose. They had another kind of aircraft with which they could have flown the Pacific. They had the Sunderland, a flying boat which was capable of operating out of Vancouver in the warm waters of the Pacific through the winter.
We have recently seen in the newspapers that this wonderful new aircraft in the United States will carry eighty passengers, and there has been a great deal of publicity behind it. As one who has flown Sunderlands, I should like to tell the committee that one of these aircraft took eighty people out of Greece in the dark days of 1940. I should say, eighty people and the air officer commanding's parrot. They are without a doubt the finest type of flying boat that has been developed up to the present time, with all respect to Mr. Howard Hughes and his gigantic machine.
Canada paid for these aircraft with dollars, and it was this government's policy not to bring them back here, not to take this opportunity which was open to them, as everyone informed in the business knows. In fact, as the minister is probably aware, we have been criticized by our Australian and New Zealand partners in the commonwealth for not taking the opportunity to develop our Pacific air lines as we could have done.
We are in the air age in a civil as well as a military sense. I shall have more to say about the latter when the defence estimates are before us, but in the civil age we had an opportunity, and this government have probably thrown it away for all time unless they can pick up the threads of a mismanaged job. Trans-Canada Air Lines have done well with what they had. I for one will support them in everything they try to do. I would like to see them develop still further, develop by independent-minded airmen and not by niggardly government policies. As a Progressive Conservative, I criticize the conservative policy which Canada has followed in her air operations from the close of the last, war. I cannot say too strongly to the government in this house:	You have lost an
opportunity, a great opportunity. You had the crews; you had the men; you had the aircraft. You discouraged the men and threw away the machines.	-
It will be remembered that a year ago I spoke in this house about airmen trying to 83166-334
get a licence to service aircraft, to operate radios to fly in this country, but by some means or another the Department of Transport managed to discourage these men.
I will say, in closing, that the government will have to operate with great energy to pick up this lost opportunity. I feel that in one way this is a criticism of public enterprise versus private enterprise. If you had given the initiative to some of the men who knew what could be done in this country, which is so adaptable in every way to air development, you might be in a better position than you are in today.

I should not allow these
remarks to go unchallenged. I am fully aware of the splendid record my hon. friend has a military flier, but the remarks he has made indicate clearly the difference between military flying and commercial flying. My hon. friend obviously would proceed without any regard whatever to earning or to balance sheets. If the hon. member for Trinity could persuade-
Mr. Chairman-

Just a minute. I did not interrupt you. Suppose you keep your seat until I have finished. If my hon. friend could persuade some of his colleagues who appear in the committee on railways and shipping to discuss the T.C.A. balance sheet, to adopt his view point, we might develop flying in this country on other lines, but we do try to keep on the basis of commercial operation.
My hon. friend says that we could have got plenty of Lancasters, and flown them across the Atlantic or the Pacific. Well, we have some Lancastrians the equal of anyone's Lancastrian planes. We used them for five years to cross the Atlantic. I would hardly wish to operate them under present conditions of competition. At the time we were operating our Lancastrians, the rates were double the present rates and we managed to break even in operating the service. To attempt to carry passengers at S325 from Montreal to London in a Lancastrian would not be profitable. I can assure my hon. friend that he could not possibly make fifty per cent of his operating expenses.
The hon. member speaks of lost opportunities to buy aircraft, and he speaks of the Sunderland.
You owned them.

No one would seriously
attempt to operate a Sunderland flying boat commercially, especially from Canada. The

Su pply- T ransport

weight of the boat calls for a tremendously excessive amount of gasoline to be burned per passenger, and the icing conditions on both coasts-let us not forget that we have such conditions on the Pacific as well as the Atlantic-would make Sunderlands unsafe as a means of transportating passengers to and from Canada.
The hon. member mentions lack of equipment. I would point out that we are supposed to be in equal partnership with the United Kingdom in operating from Canada to the United Kingdom, and I believe that at the present time we are carrying at least seventy per cent of the traffic against their thirty per cent. Why? Because we have more equipment.
We underestimated, it is true, the potential traffic on the north Atlantic, or at least our share of it. Had we anticipated running in excess of eleven trips a week, which we never expected at this stage of our development, we would have had more trained crews. The bottle-neck in the Atlantic is not equipment but crews. We could make many more trips with the aeroplanes than we have crews available. We are building up our operating staff as rapidly as we can. I expect to be censured next year for having too much equipment. If anyone happened to ask me what I will do with all these planes T.C.A. has on order I could not tell him, but we have always been short of equipment. We had a chance to buy exceptionally fine planes at a reasonable price. We bought twenty. If we can keep twenty North Stars busy we shall be in international aviation in a big way.
As regards refusing licences to returned airmen, I have said we have ten times as many men in aviaiton today as in 1939, all with licences and all with suitable outlets for their energies, all making a bit of money, which I do not think was a bad achievement. I do not mind fair criticism and accurate criticism, but I have never heard a man talk about civil aviation who obviously knew so little about the problems to be encountered in that direction.

The minister has challenged me on technical grounds and I am willing to reply to him on technical grounds. His first criticism was about the numbers of aircraft. If he will recall it, he himself this afternoon said that he could use on the north Atlantic run twice the number of aircraft he has at the present time.
If I had the crews.

I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the chaotic system under which the administration and the control of radio and broadcasting are being continued under three departments and two ministers when common sense would dictate that the administration should be brought under one department and one minister. In saying what I am about to say I do not ' intend to enter into the subject matter of the final report which was tabled earlier this evening from the radio committee, or the earlier report which came from that committee and which was tabled in the house last Friday evening. I am informed that the government has given an undertaking that full opportunity will be afforded the house to discuss those reports on a suitable occasion this week. Therefore hon. members may be assured that in forgoing the opportunity to discuss more widely the question of radio broadcasting at this time, they are not forgoing that opportunity for the entire session. This matter is of such leading importance that this house has no right to prorogue without having discussed it fully. In view of that undertaking which I understand the government has given I shall confine my remarks to certain aspects of the situation created by the present system of administration and control by the government.
Radio and broadcasting at the present time are regulated under two statutes of this parliament, the Broadcasting Act of 1936 and the Radio Act of 1938. Under both of those acts certain functions were assigned to the minister named in each act, and it happens that in the case of both acts the minister named was the Minister of Transport. We have the amazing situation today that the hon. gentleman who holds the portfolio of Minister of Transport has nothing to do either with the functions assigned to the Minister of Transport under the Radio Act or with the functions assigned to tfie Minister of Transport under the Broadcasting Act.
The effect of the Broadcasting Act of 1936 was to give certain functions and powers to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and also to the Minister of Transport. The effect of the Radio Act of 1938 was to give the Minister of Transport the power to license radio stations. He alone is the fountain of licences for broadcasting in Canada. Under the present system he seeks the advice and recommendations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; but, as I say, he is the sole fountain of licences. His radio division has been ordered by the government to carry on this form of administration.

The committee will recall that when these acts were passed the present Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) was Minister of Transport. When the war came along and he was appointed Minister of Munitions and Supply he took with him certain functions of the Minister of Transport, even though he wras relinquishing the portfolio of transport,. He took with him the functions assigned under both these acts to the Minister of Transport.
There followed a series of orders in council under which jurisdiction which was vested by these two acts in the Minister of Transport was juggled, with this curious result. First, we had order in council 3076, dated July 8, 1940, which provided that the duties, powers and functions vested in the Minister of Transport under various acts, and the radio services of the Department of Transport under the Broadcasting Act of 1936, were transferred to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. The next order in council was 3435, dated July 25, 1940, which conferred upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply the duties, powers and functions vested in the Minister of Transport under the Radio Act of 1938. Then came order in council 8207. dated October 24, 1944, under which the duties, powers' and functions in respect to the radio services, Department of Transport, and under the Radio Act of 1938 and other acts, were transferred to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. There was a further order in council, P.C. 6552, dated October 18, 1945, under which the functions of the Minister of Transport under the Broadcasting Act were conferred upon the minister who was Minister of National War Services and who is today the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). The portfolio of national war services being in course of liquidation, we can expect a further order in council vesting in the Minister of National Revenue the powers assigned to the Minister of Transport under the Broadcasting Act.
That situation is a hodgepodge. There are three departments involved and two ministers. We have the curious anomaly where the minister now holding the portfolio of transport has nothing to do with two important branches of the Department of Transport, the one which we discussed earlier this evening, namely, air services, including civil aviation and meteorological services, and, second, this radio division. It is anomalous also that the control of radio, including the licensing of stations for the purposes of broadcasting, should be vested in one minister, and then that other jurisdiction should be vested in still another minister by the act which establishes the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and gives it its sweeping

powers, including its powers over private broadcasting in Canada. I urge upon the committee that 'that anomaly should not be allowed to continue. If the right hon. gentleman who holds the portfolio of reconstruction and supply is, with the will of the government, to continue to hold and exercise the functions of Minister of Transport in respect of the Radio Act of 1938 and the functions of the Minister of Transport in respect of air service, it would certainly seem to be the part of common sense that the functions of the Minister of Transport under the Broadcasting Act of 1938 now exercised by the Minister of National War Services, who is now the Minister of National Revenue, should also be vested in the right hon. gentleman who holds the portfolio of reconstruction and supply. That anomaly and that puzzling situation constitute I submit, a source of constant confusion. The confusion is evident among hon. members in the questions they ask from time to time in the house. The situation is confusing also to members of the radio committee, and it is high time 'that the government take the matter in hand and take the sensible course of bringing both jurisdictions, namely jurisdiction under the Radio Act and under the Broadcasting Act, under the one minister.
Here is the situation that was recently before the radio committee in a very striking form. It is quite possible that government policy may lead in one direction in respect of the administration of the Broadcasting Act by one minister and that it may lead in quite a .different direction through the other minister, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, in respect of the licensing functions he enjoys under the Radio Act.

The minister has indicated that he has not seen the brief since the issue arose in the committee and that it does not represent his views or government policy. Do I understand that there is no government policy opposed to vesting in an independent regulatory board or tribunal the regulatory functions of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation over private stations under the Broadcasting Act and licensing powers of the minister under the Radio Act, and that government policy is not opposed to vesting these powers in an independent regulatory board?

I have been a member of the government for a considerable period and a fairly regular attendant at meetings of council. and I have never heard the government asked to express a policy on that, nor have I ever seen a report indicating why a policy should be expressed. The policy on broadcasting is a function of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Unless the government is asked for a decision by the corporation, it has been in the past, and, I think, will be in the future, quite satisfied to leave the matter of broadcasting policy to the corporation.

One further question
arising out of the minister's answer. May I ask the minister whether he has any objection or sees any obstacle in the way of his taking over the functions of the minister under the Broadcasting Act. If he is to continue to exercise the functions of the minister under the Radio Act, is there any reason why he should not also exercise the functions of minister under the Broadcasting Act?

There is no reason why I should or should not. There is no relation between the two functions. There is no relation between the administration of the Radio Act and the administration of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At one time I was administering both, when I was Minister of Transport and subsequently for a time. During the war it was considered wise-and I agreed with the decision-that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should report to another minister. There is absolutely no reason why it should report to the minister who administers the Radio Act.
I rise to say a word in the present discussion since I am on the radio committee and take a good deal of interest in my work there.
