There is one important and, I believe, serious matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries with respect to which I am going to ask him that between now and next session every possible investigation be made and steps be taken to prevent what I claim is a menace to the fisheries of the Fraser river. But before dealing with that one specific question which I have in mind tonight, may I draw to the minister's attention some of the communications which I received following a speech I made in this house a short time ago when the Fisheries Research Board Act was under review.
It was a good speech.

Thank you. At that time I dealt particularly with the quality of fish, amongst other matters. Following a report of my speech which appeared in many newspapers, I received, in all, thirty-five to forty letters; and invariably the writers, whilst reminding me that quality was essential to the consumption of more fish, pointed out, each and every one of them, that price was just as important a factor, if not more so, in increasing the consumption of fish. I wish to put one of those letters on record tonight,
and I do so because I think the minister will agree that, while we must go after quality, nevertheless something more must be done than has been done to make fish cheaper and more readily available, particularly to those living in the interior provinces. This is one of the many letters that came to me:

In the Saskatoon Star issue of April 23, you are wondering why the public does not eat more seafood. Perhaps a few price quotations will

There is really no object in spending a great deal of money in an educational campaign unless prices come down or purses are better filled. Then you won't need a campaign of any sort. I like fish and would rather eat it than meat, but my budget won't allow it too often.
That was the gist of the majority of the letters I received, following the debate in this house on the Fisheries Research Board Act. I am bringing them to the minister's attention to emphasize that some steps will have to be taken by his department, and the industry as well will have to be reminded that fish must be distributed .more abundantly and more cheaply than is the case at the present time.
My particular reason for rising at this time is to bring to the minister's attention what I claim is a serious menace to the salmon industry of the Fraser river. In fact, if no steps are taken in the matter it is my opinion that we face in the near future the depletion of the salmon industry on the Fraser river.
It may interest the members of the committee to know that the great Columbia river to the south of us in British Columbia, which has its head waters in that province but its outlet in the United States, was once the great salmon river of the Pacific coast. But dams were built on that river in the state of Washington to develop hydro-electric power, and on three occasions I raised my voice in this house drawing to the attention of the government, both Conservative and Liberal, that by simply closing our eyes and
Supply-Fisheries

remaining silent we had lost a great fisheries heritage through the building of dams on the Columbia river by the United States. Away back in 1845 there had been entered into between Great Britain and the United States an agreement which contained a clause stipulating that the Columbia river, which rises in British Columbia, was to be free of access to all British and Canadian citizens. But when the United States started to build dams on the Columbia river for hydro-electric power no voice was raised at that time by the government of Canada to maintain the rights which were given to us by that treaty. I may inform the minister, although it is too late to tell him now, that when the hearings were being held in the state of Washington at the time these dams were projected, those who had to do with the fisheries in the state of Washington firmly believed that the voice of Canada would be heard in protest against the building of these dams for power development.
What has been t'he effect? I had the pleasure of visiting one of these dams where there is a fishway or ladder which cost seven and a half million dollars to build. That fishway, it is true, takes the salmon up over the dam. Ever since, the United States authorities have been trying to bolster up the whole project with figures and statistics. They have men engaged in what they call a counting-house where machines are used to count the fish and classify the various species or varieties. The machines operate very much like a typewriter. The fish travel over a white table and the men who are sitting above the table can easily see the fish through a glass floor, and they know the varieties, and hence can make a fairly accurate count of the fish passing up the river. Every year they can show the great numbers of salmon that go up over the dam. For many years they have been endeavouring to put across the idea that this fishway was a success, owing to the numbers of salmon which were able to go up the river and which previously could not go over the hydro-electric dams. I can tell hon. members, and I wane the minister to remember this-
Will the hon. member please tell us which hydro-electric dam?

I am speaking particularly of the one at Bonneville in the state of Washington. They .constructed there a $7,500,000 fishway to take the salmon up around the dam; but in all the dams that they have built to take the fish up, that is, but one aspect of the situation, for they have never been able to find a way to bring the little fingerlings 
down successfully, and those who know tell us that the Columbia river is doomed. It is doomed because, after ten years of research, they have never been able to discover how to bring the fry or little fish down over the dams or through the turbines without great mortality. The result is that the fishway in the Columbia river will in time be of no use in that regard. It will be only a matter of time until there will be no fish left in the Columbia river.
The fish would have to come up over the Grand Coulee dam and come down through the turbines.
The Grand Coulee dam is too high.
How do they get them through?

They do not go through; it stops them. The dam blocks them; but on the Bonneville farther down the river they built a fishway at the cost which I have just mentioned, which is able to take the fish up over the dam; but as I said a moment ago-and I wish to repeat it-they have never been able to bring the small fry down successfully. It is estimated that every year the small fry die by the millions; consequently, in spite of the fish going up to spawn, the fishery actually is decreasing.
Is it a fact that, the fish do not get up to British Columbia to spawn at all?

The hon. member is right. Since the dams were built on the Columbia, no fish are now going up in British Columbia. We lost the entire fishery in the interior of British Columbia by the building of dams, and no protest was made by any Canadian government, although we had a right to protest under the treaty of 1845.
I shall now deal with what I particularly wanted to say, namely, the menace to the Fraser river. In 1938, the province of British Columbia had a survey made of the potential water power of the Fraser river. I shall quote what was said:
When the demand arises, the waters of the Fraser river are capable of furnishing over six million horse-power.
They put out a little booklet-hon. members from British Columbia may have seen it-called "Water. Powers, Fraser River, British Columbia." In this report of the power commission of British Columbia there is outlined all the potential hydro-electric development of the Fraser river watershed. Almost each page shows the spot where hydro-

Supply-F isheries
electric power could he developed. Those having to do with fisheries view with alarm the building of dams on the Fraser river. Let me say that, speaking as a member of the international salmon fisheries commission, we realize, as a commission, that dams will have to be built on the river for the development of electric power. We are not entirely against the construction of dams. Our engineers have also made a survey of the waters of the Fraser river,-and we have discovered that there are great areas to which no fish go. There are other areas to which the fish go, and therein, we believe, lies the danger.
Beginning a year or two ago, the British Columbia Electric Company started with a project on the Bridge river which I think is to be completed this year. Most hon. members from British Columbia have received a copy of the "Construction World". In that booklet is outlined the great project of hydroelectric development on Bridge river. An 800-foot reservoir dam is being constructed. They are raising the level of one lake forty feet and taking the water through a penstock many miles, thereby developing power for electricity. No intimation has been given by the company to the fisheries department of what the effect might be. May I point out to the committee that when the British Columbia Electric constructed a dam at Stave lake some years ago, certain streams were completely dried out and the salmon that used to go up these streams disappeared. The report now is that they may now abandon this dam after the Bridge river project is completed. But may I point out to the committee that when they built the Stave lake dam and put in the project there, no protest of any kind was made either by the provincial or dominion government or by their officials against the building of the dam.
What year was that?

I am not sure. If my memory serves me correctly it was back in 1925 or 1926. I think it was around that time. No protest of any kind was made, and I claim there was a great loss to the salmon industry.
If the sockeye salmon comes back to its once great value on the Fraser river, as we hope and expect it will-I mean to the extent which it was in 1913 at the time the slide occurred, and which it is the duty of the commission of which I have the honour to be a member to endeavour to bring about, and we are working to that end-it will mean an annual return of between 835 million and $40 million. In 1913 two and a half million cases of sockeye salmon were canned from the salmon that went up the Fraser river to the
headwaters of that river in the interior. After the disaster of 1913-14, of course the decline took place; but we are hopeful that, before long, we shall be able to bring back that great fishing industry.
To what does the hon. member refer?

I refer to the disaster that took place when the contractors were building the Canadian National Railways through the mountains to Vancouver. They blasted hundreds of thousands of tons of rock into a place on the Fraser river called Hell's Gate canyon. In the spring of 1914 a slide also took place. In the year that they blasted the rock into the canyon millions of sockeye salmon were unable to pass up the gorge and so died without spawning. Since 1913 the industry has gone down and down. In 1937 the commission was set up to overcome the difficulty. That, however, is a story all by itself and would take an entire evening to tell.
I am dealing particularly with the menace of the water-power development, and I suggest to the minister that he look at what is now being done in the United States. It is true they are doing this in the United States after some disaster has befallen the fishing industry. I shall read to the minister the laws of the state of Washington. I realize that he may probably have to consult writh the province of British Columbia. Someone in the dominion government should, however, approach the province and have a law something like this put into effect. I quote from the "Annotated Laws relating to Food and Shell Fish 1945" of the state of Washington.
In the event that any person, firm, corporation or government agency desires to construct any form of hydraulic project or other project that will use. divert, obstruct or change the natural flow or bed of any river or stream or that will utilize any of the waters of the state or materials from the stream beds, such person, firm, corporation or government agency shall submit to the department of fisheries and the department of game full plans and specifications of their proposed construction or work, complete plans and specifications for the proper protection of fish life in connection therewith.
I want to compare that with what we have in our law today. We have nothing like that to prevent the building of dams, but we have something which many years ago might have acted, I presume fairly well, although some of us have doubted it. If you take the revised statutes of Canada and refer to the Fisheries Act you will find that section 31 merely states this:
Every slide, dam or other obstruction across or in any stream where the minister determines it to be necessary for the public interest that a fish-pass should exist, shall be provided by
Supply-Fisheries

the owner or occupier with a durable and efficient fishway or canal around the slide, dam or other obstruction which shall be maintained in a good and effective condition by said owner or occupier in such place and of such form and capacity as will in the opinion of the minister satisfactorily permit the free passage of fish through the same.
That was in 1927. I claim that that law is antiquated and is useless in the face of the potential dangers confronting us on the Fraser river. The present section will come into operation only after the dam has been built, and if, in the opinion of the minister, a fish-pass is required he can then order the company to build one. That is hardly good enough because, once the dam is up, the damage may well have been done, as it may take only one year to wipe out a fishery valued at many thousands of dollars.
Let me point out another danger on the Fraser river and, I suppose, on other rivers as well, and that is the dredging which is taking place. There was dredging for gold at a place called Quesnel many years ago. On the Quesnel system we estimate that we have one [DOT] of the greatest potential sockeye salmon streams in the entire Fraser river watershed. In 1912 or 1913 some four million sockeye salmon went into that area, and last year, by actual count, there were only around 685, or a drop from four million to 685. In other words, that area has been practically wiped out. In consequence of the gold mining company going there with a mammoth dredge and expending many millions of dollars in dredging, they have blocked rivers and lakes. No steps were taken to have them remove the gravel. The damage has been done and now it is our duty as a commission to endeavour to bring that area back to what is was in 1912. If the department of the day had been fairly active or had had some power such as I have cited from the laws of the state of Washington, steps could have been taken immediately against such an operation or company.
I contend that our laws will have to be amended and brought up to date, because we stand in grave danger, on the Fraser river at least, of the entire fishery being wiped out.
Let me bring another instance to the attention of the minister, and this one is nearer home. A certain project is being carried out by the dominion at Pemberton Meadows. They started work early in March of this year. If that work had been carried out as intended, they were going to dig a canal and divert the river. If they had proceeded with that we would have lost one of the finest spawning beds in that area, one that usually harbours some thirty thousand sockeye salmon. By

good luck we were able to get hold of the engineer, and when the matter was drawn to his attention he was good enough to order that the work be discontinued until a complete survey could be made as to its effect.
I mention this particularly to the minister in order to bring it forcibly to his attention that there is no protection at present against digging canals, gold mine dredging or the construction of hydraulic dams. There is some protection, seemingly, in the act, that if a dam is built and it is found to be to the detriment of the fishing industry the minister can take certain steps.

I am very much interested in what the hon. member is saying, because he is perhaps the best-posted member in the house on this subject. According to what he now says, if they are to build dams on the Fraser river, I believe the whole fishing industry there will go to pieces, because on the Columbia the Grand Coulee is 550 feet high and fish cannot go up that dam, and the same will happen on the Fraser river.

Everyone knows the high
pressure sort of propaganda campaign that can be put on by a company that wishes to construct a dam across a stream for the development of electrical power, especially if the people in the area are not receiving any benefit from the salmon on the river. It can be pointed out that there would be cheap electricity for the farms and industrial power for those who wish to go into industry. A beautiful picture can be painted to the people generally and I fear that in a campaign of that kind the fishing industry may suffer and become the victim of such propaganda. I am calling this matter to the attention of the minister in time, as I believe, and I submit that it is time steps were taken before any great development or building of dams takes place. I doubt whether one of his officers has been up to see what effect the Bridge river project may have on the salmon industry on the Fraser river.
May I ask the hon. member whether his commission has registered any complaint to the minister?

We have protested for the past five years to the provincial government. We have asked the provincial government on every occasion if they would be good enough to consult with us, to present their plans to us and give us a chance to look at them before going ahead with the work. But although we have requested that, and had an assurance from the premier that that would be done, so far it has not been done Fortunately or

Supply-Fisheries
unfortunately, these works are carried out by officials, and since the province of British Columbia, like certain other provinces, do not control their fisheries, perhaps they are not as much interested as they might be if they had the control, as the province of Quebec and some other provinces have.. I believe the province of Saskatchewan controls its fisheries, but we in British Columbia do not control ours. The fisheries come exclusively under the dominion, and therefore the province may not be so much concerned. There is sitting in Victoria a little group of men who are power-minded'

I say that advisedly-their thoughts being for the development of hydroelectric power on the Fraser river, and they have no thought whatsoever of what effect the building of these dams may have on the fishing industry.
The fishing industry is so valuable to British Columbia that we cannot sit idly by without taking proper steps and putting in the proper safeguards now. What I suggest to the minister is that every department, both provincial and federal, before proceeding with projects of that kind, and private industry as well, should be required to place their plans before the fisheries department and so give them a chance to find out what effect these projects will have on the fishing industry.
There is a principle or, at any rate, a precedent that we can act upon. Neither a provincial government nor a private individual can construct a bridge over a navigable river unless, first of all, the project is approved by the Department of Public Works. There you have a precedent, and if that safeguard is provided to take care of shipping, surely we should be more concerned or, at any rate, as much concerned about an industry that gives employment to thousands of men and is worth many millions of dollars.
I am asking the minister to give serious thought to the matter between now and the next session of parliament, and to take steps to see what can be done so that in future we shall not witness on the Fraser river what has taken place on the Columbia.
Am I to understand that the provincial government would permit the damming of the Fraser river, which I believe is a navigable water, without con. sultation with the government?

There is issued by the provincial government a booklet in which the entire Fraser river is outlined, giving the places they recommend should be used for the development of hydro-electric power, and Bridge river is named in this booklet. That is the first one that is being proceeded with.

I am merely asking the question for information. My understanding is that the Fraser river is navigable. Surely the federal government has control of that, has it not? The famous beaver we hear so much about went up there and the whole development of Canada other than Ontario was through the Fraser river. If it is not navigable, I do not know what it is.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext: We all certainly have enjoyed listening to the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster in connection with the damage which may be caused to the fisheries of the Fraser river and in British Columbia by virtue of the possible development of hydro-electric power. I have not had an opportunity to make a full and complete study of the legislation which now exists in regard to the construction of fishways and dams for this purpose. I would point out, however, to the hon. member the fact that the present act under which we are now functioning is the Fisheries Act of 1932. It is quite possible that in section 20 of the Fisheries Act of 1932, which contains some ten sections, there may be some powers which the minister now has, but which he did not have under the old revised statutes of Canada which were passed in 1927. I would, however, assure the hon. member most sincerely that, so far as I am concerned, if the legislation as it now exists is deficient, having regard to the proper protection of the salmon fisheries, I and the officials of my department will certainly make a careful study of the matter between now and the next session and see what can be done.

I should like to invite the attention of the committee for a few minutes to the fisheries problems on the east coast. At this late stage I hesitate to take up the time of the committee, but when one realizes the proportions which the fisheries are assuming in our economic life, I feel that the subject merits all the consideration we can direct to it from the people of Canada generally. The solution to the immediate problems facing the fishing industry lies with the people of Canada themselves in the way of increased consumption, as was brought out in a recent debate. Therefore, I feel it is a problem which is of great concern to each and every person in Canada. For that reason I feel we are justified in asking the committee to bear with us for a short time even at this late date.
At the outset I should like to say that, from the point of view of the industry on the east coast, the past year has been one of development as far as the relationships
Supply-Fisheries

between the industry and the department go. We feel that, in the dying days of the last session, we had in this house a good debate and one which was constructive. Since that time the department has embarked on a wide programme of reorganization which has certainly benefited the department and the industry. We feel that a great deal of credit is due the minister who has applied himself with such great vigour and constructiveness to the problems facing the industry. We are now looking hopefully to the new deputy minister who has shown, by his ability in such matters as assisting the industry through the recent support announcement made by the minister, that the department is certainly on the right track.
The first problem I should like to draw to the attention of the committee tonight is an international one, and it has to do with the general problem of depletion. The hon. member for New Westminster ably brought to the attention of the committee tonight the matter of the depletion of salmon from the great salmon rivers of British Columbia. I am concerned with the depletion of deep sea fish on the Grand Bank and other banks off the coast of Nova Scotia, involving principally the fishing industries in the United States and Canada. The minister is well aware of the situation. It has been brought to his attention a number of times, both through his own departmental channels and through the industry. I know he has a sympathetic feeling toward the problem. Recently, on July 4, the question was brought to the attention of the government by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs at page 5080 of Hansard indicated that he is fully aw7are of the scope and difficulty of the problem and its solution. The problem arises out of the fact that the modern way of deep-sea fishing is by means of dragging or trawling, whereby draggers tow behind them a net which scoops up fish more or less indiscriminately. It is a method which is directly opposed in that respect to the old-fashioned and still existing method of dory fishing, which is a hook-and-line propostion and is, therefore, more selective. There is no doubt that this dragging method does destroy a wide variety of types and sizes of fish. At the present time one difficulty is associated with the fact that there is sufficient codfish on the market. The inventories are high. Some countries, particularly the United States, have little or no demand for fresh codfish. The accent and emphasis is on fresh haddock. The result is that many of the draggers, which catch cod in greater quantities than 
they catch haddock, are forced to dispose of their cod whilst still at sea. The United States has always adopted a reasonable attitude toward this problem. It is the nature of the industry that it is destructive. There is no intent on their part to deplete the banks. I would', however, again urge this government to do whatever they can by way of negotiation with the United States to see if some reasonable understanding cannot be arrived at to avoid the depletion which will so greatly affect the industry in the future.
Then there is the matter of the continental shelf, which was raised last year by the hon. member for New Westminster and emphasized during the debate on the fisheries estimates, in the last session of this parliament. That problem has not been solved. Our fishermen are still encountering destruction of their gear and running the hazard of having their ships destroyed, with the attendant loss of life, on what we have always considered to be our very own banks off the coast of Nova Scotia. I refer particularly to the Banquereau or, as it is otherwise called, the Quero bank. I would again ask the minister if he would seek some avenue for approaching the other nations involved in this fishing problem on the coast of Nova Scotia and try to come to some understanding and create regulations which will circumvent this hazard to our own fisheries.
Before proceeding farther, I should like to say that we feel there is a need for a further extension of the protective service we have off the coast of Nova Scotia. In my particular part of the province, the constituency of Quecns-Lunenburg, the only protective craft we have immediately available is one known as the Gilbert, which is entirely inadequate. The accommodation in this boat is poor. It would certainly be well worth the department's while to look into the matter of providing a replacement craft for the outmoded Gilbert.
There is the new air-sea rescue service which we feel fits nicely into the programme of protective service, and so far there are good indications that it is performing the function it was intended to perform. There have been one or two instances, however, where the service was slow in going to the rescue of craft which it deemed to be not in immediate danger. The craft in one instance, and I believe in two, was drifting helplessly, and the protective service, when it was got in touch with, is reported to have said the craft was in no immediate danger. The craft in question were rudderless and had no radios. It is pretty difficult to convince seamen at the height of a storm, on small craft, that they are in no immediate danger. If the

Supply-Fisheries
obstacle is towage; if the matter of competing with private enterprise for towage is the consideration, then I feel that at least the protective service should stand by in case of danger, to see that there is no loss of life.
I should like also to repeat our oft-presented demands that further consideration be given the question of breakwaters and wharves, which are such an important feature of any fishing community. There is a great economy drive on now, and we know that government expenditure is to be cut to the minimum; but I think the minister must urge that discretion be exercised and see that the wrong emphasis is not applied to cut dowm the number of wharves and breakwaters. I would urge also that more dredging be done, because inshore fishermen simply cannot operate without dredging and the dredges available on the coasts of Xova Scotia are entirely inadequate.
As various hon. members informed this house during the debate on the Fisheries Research Board Act, the industry is in a difficult position brought about by the conversion from a wartime to a peacetime economy. Without going into this matter fully again I desire merely to state that war-produced changes in the markets for our fish placed more emphasis on frozen fish than had been the case up to that time. In addition, heavy demands for food occasioned by the war made it necessary to produce fish in larger quantities than ever before. Now reconversion to a peacetime economy means that we must revert to our old markets, which in many cases are no longer available to us because of increased competition. We may also be obliged to place more emphasis on salt and pickled fish, as was the case prior to the war, rather than on fresh fish. This was thoroughly covered in the minister's statement on June 24, in which he announced that up to 88,000,900 would be made available to support the fishing industry for the remainder of this year. The industry was very grateful for the programme of relief feeding outlined in the minister's report. Under the Fisheries Prices Support Act, funds will be made available for engaging in an extensive programme of education which should increase the consumption of fish in Canada. When we realize that the fishing industry in the United States has been ttying for some time to raise a fund of half a million dollars to embark upon a programme of education within that country, the industry realizes how fortunate it is to have the government come forward with this offer of assistance.
An analysis of the minister's statement will clearly indicate where the difficulty lies in our industiy at the present time. For relief
feeding the government is prepared to buy sizeable quantities of dried, pickled and canned fish, but for various reasons it cannot see its way clear to purchase frozen fish for the same purpose. To deal with the east coast, this boils down to the fact that the government's programme of relief feeding, with the exception of the canning industry, provides support for that phase of the industry which could best get along without it, and makes it necessary to find other means of supporting the fresh fish industry, which is the only part of the industry left in real difficulty after the relief feeding programme is implemented. The minister's solution of this problem is to implement the Fisheries Prices Support Act to permit the government to buy frozen fillets, and to recommend that the industry divert as much raw codfish as possible to salting rather than freezing. I wish to emphasize that on the east coast the codfishing involving fresh fillets is the only phase of the industry in real difficulty. That is the only item which is giving us any concern; our other problems in tire fishing industry are considerably in the future.
The minister's statement presents several outstanding difficulties with which the department is fully familiar. As in the past the industry will adjust its own production to suit outstanding demands, and there will be some diversion of cod into the salt fish industry. But too much should not be expected in this direction, because refrigeration and other facilities were built during the war at great cost to accommodate an expanded demand for fresh fish, and it would seem to many a retrograde step to leave these facilities idle to any great extent if it is possible to find other solutions. A second outstanding difficulty would be encountered by the government in selling domestically the frozen fish it would buy under the Fisheries Prices Support Act. At the present time, speaking very approximately, there are two and a half million pounds of frozen cod fillets in existing inventories, and it is estimated that, under normal circumstances of production and in the light of present markets, this surplus will rise to approximately ten million pounds over the next eight to ten months. This means that the government will be faced with the necessity of purchasing and disposing of approximately ten million pounds of frozen cod fillets. This programme will involve all the difficulties of storage, transportation, financing, merchandizing and so on. However, it is assumed that by the end of the period I have mentioned, from eight to ten months, this reconversion phase will be completed and
Supply-Fisheries

the industry will know what its markets are, so that it will be able to gauge its production accordingly.
There would appear to be a much more direct solution to this problem than government purchasing, a solution which the industry on the east coast would much prefer. However, in view of the international monetary situation the solution I have in mind is dependent upon the availability of Canadian funds in foreign fish-consuming countries. The invoking of the Fisheries Prices Support Act naturally gives the impression that there is no export demand for frozen cod fillets, but this is not the case. There are known to be demands in England, France and Italy, and it may be that there are demands elsewhere. We know that inquiries have been received from representatives of these three countries seeking to work out an arrangement to buy cod fillets. The obstacle is that these countries lack Canadian dollars. The industry itself is confident that it can find the markets and can readily circumvent such problems as transportation, storage and distribution, because it has well-established channels. The quantity of fish involved is approximately ten million pounds, and this quantity can be absorbed in these three countries where people are ready and able to pay for it in the currency of their own country. This would not be a programme of relief feeding. The cost of the amount of fish involved would certainly not be more than $1,500,000. There is no certainty that the countries concerned, England, France and Italy, would accept loans to buy fish, but we in the maritimes feel that this is an approach to the problem that should be fully explored.
It seems clear to the industry and to all in the maritimes that the direct solution to this problem would be to make loans available to these three countries in the amount required to purchase the approximately ten million pounds of fish that are likely to be surplus over the next eight to ten months, rather than to have the government use the same amount of money to purchase those fish and attempt to have them consumed domestically in a market which at the present time must be considered somewhat doubtful. When I say that I do not mean in any sense that I believe the consuming capacity of the Canadian public is doubtful, because I am strongly of the opinion that, with an intensive programme of education and inspection to ensure a good quality being on the market, the per capita consumption in Canada will increase sufficiently to take care of our present surpluses.

The government may take the stand that it has gone as far as it proposes to go in the matter of making loans available to foreign countries, but we in the maritimes do not see the justification for that stand. In the first place, the government is making the money available anyhow. In the second place, as has been pointed out previously in this house, the maritimes have benefited from the government's heavy loan programme less than any region in Canada to date. The returns to the maritime provinces from the hundreds of millions of dollars lent to foreign countries have been infinitesimal when compared with the returns to Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia; and when one considers the contracts for wheat, beef, and other farm products which bring good returns to the western provinces, it must be conceded that the maritime provinces have not fared at all well in this programme of external trade.
In a speech in the house at an earlier date I showed that, of the total amount of $330,872,575 in contracts awarded against these loans by the Canadian Commercial Corporation and the Canadian export board as of March of this year, Nova Scotia benefited to the extent of only $2,151,351 or -65 per cent. The three maritime provinces together benefited to the extent of only -76 per cent, whereas they comprise ten per cent of the total population. In this particular instance, we are not asking for additional funds; the funds are there anyhow; we are asking, however, that the funds be rediverted to be made available as a further loan rather than for the purpose of government purchase of fish for domestic use. There are many advantages accruing from the foreign loans approach to the problem which are self-evident, the most obvious being that this programme would permit the industry to stand on its own feet rather than lean on the government, and this is all to the good. It would also serve the important purpose of letting it maintain valuable contacts and markets abroad, which it already has. Furthermore, it would save the government all the difficulties involved in purchasing large quantities of fresh fish and disposing of them domestically.
I feel quite certain that 'the other maritime member's feel the same as I do in this respect. My colleague the hon. member for Vancouver North says that the British Columbia members feel that way, too. I did not wish to give the impression that the industry is not appreciative of the government's splendid offer of assistance. I am sure the industry fully appreciates that offer, and every fisherman in the industry on the east coast will appreciate

Supply-Fisheries
this government's willingness to come to the industry's assistance when trouble arises.
We have no criticism of the government's action at all; we are merely trying to suggest how funds already available may be used to the best possible advantage of the industry and with the least difficulty to the department.
I would say, in conclusion, that this fund of 38 million to be made available by the government for relief feeding is a great boost or "shot in the arm" for the fishing industry on the east coast. The industry, as we are aware, is facing problems which are growing more difficult. Fish prices took a small slump, and there was some indication that they would take a further slide because of mounting inventories. This offer of assistance through the channels of relief feeding and the Fisheries Prices Support Act is the impetus the industry needs at the present time.
Mr. MoLURE: Mr. Chairman, I know how anxious the minister is to have his estimates passed, and for that reason I am not going to make any extended remarks. I shall discuss the different items in which I am interested when they are reached. We have listened to two excellent speeches, one from the west and one from the maritime provinces. I was, however, disappointed that the Minister of Fisheries did not, as usual, give his excellent address respecting the policy and the organization of his department. Probably he was in a hurry to have his estimates passed and did not make those observations this year, as has been his custom.
On this item I should like to ask him about the allocation in connection with the $8 million which will be spent on relief feeding and for the fishermen of the maritime provinces. Then, perhaps he would give us a statement with reference to the prices board, as to whether they are operating and whether definite floor prices or ceiling prices have been put on lobsters for the season.
I would ask from him a report respecting the fishing season on lobsters, which is now, at least in part, closed for the maritime provinces. I shall not speak at length because I realize that all hon. members are anxious to have the estimates passed, and I realize that under the different items I shall have an opportunity to say what I have in mind.
This seems to be fish day in the House of Commons.
I should like to have an answer.
I can answer the questions on the different items as they come up.

I have listened attentively to the hon. member for New Westminster, who told us a wonderful story about sockeye salmon. I listened to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg tell us about cod and haddock, and the hon, member for Queens tell us about fish in the waters of Prince Edward Island.
I would remind the committee, however, that we have some excellent fish in the prairie provinces. I would refer to the Winnipeg goldeye and the lake Winnipeg whitefish. We do not trouble the dominion government so far as the care of these fish is concerned. The provincial government looks after the matter. Would the minister be good enough to do as his predecessor did, namely, to give me a report respecting the work done in connection with the whitefish in lake Winnipeg so that [DOT] I may use that information when I return to my constituency.
We have reports from the national research board. They are not confined to lake Winnipeg alone, but deal with research work in all the prairie lakes.
This is research carried out by the minister's department with respect to whitefish. He will know what I mean.
I shall be glad to give that information.

Mr. Chairman, may I
offer my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Fisheries upon his timely statement of June 24 when he announced the new policy of the government with respect to purchases of fish and the proclamation of the Fisheries Prices Support Act.
However, I fully concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. This policy of the government is indeed a step in the right direction, but we feel that this policy does not bring a complete solution to the most important problem of fish marketing in eastern Canada and more especially for the Gaspe region, which I have the honour to represent in this house. In his statement the hon. minister said:
The act gives the board powers to buy and sell fish and to prescribe prices. The board will be established without delay. It will confine its operations during the present fiscal year to fish produced during the remainder of the 1947 season. It will be asked to prepare in collaboration with industry a general distributional programme, including advertising, designed to increase domestic sales of fish of all species and kinds, and particularly packaged fish, and in particular to consider the specific species of the east, prairies and British Columbia in which the pricee received by fishermen
Supply-Fisheries

from the freezers are unduly low in 1947, and to devise means of maintaining these prices at or near their current levels.
This programme of support of the prices of fish for sale on the Canadian market does not, as I said a moment ago, solve the problem in my part of the country. Indeed, if the government tries to sell our fish on the domestic market our fishermen will be at a great disadvantage in comparison and in competition with the fishermen of British Columbia and of the maritime provinces. The fishing season in Gaspe lasts normally from three to four months a year, and by early December or January our frozen fish cannot compete with the fresh catches from other parts of the country. Therefore our products are not as easy to sell on the domestic market as fresh caught fish coming from other parts of Canada. What our fishermen are interested in is to regain former markets in w'orld trade. At the beginning of hostilities, and more especially at the beginning of the Ethiopian war, the Gaspe area lost its main market, which was then Italy, through the sanctions which were imposed against that country. During the last great war we sold most of our fish to UNRRA, and today, since the foreign market demand has fallen, our fishermen are faced with the fact that if they do not regain their market in Italy they will soon have either to stop fishing completely or to go into it on a part-time basis only. I am told that recently offers were received by my fishermen for quite a considerable order of fish from Italy and France; but, unfortunately, since these two countries cannot afford to pay in either Canadian or United States dollars, we cannot sell to them. In agreement with my hon. friend, the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg, I hope that the government will, without delay, study this problem, which is more of a financial nature, and try to find a solution to it.
While I am speaking on these estimates, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister some of the resolutions which were adopted at the last meeting of the organized fishermen of my county, held at Ste. Anne de la Pocat-iere on January 9, 10 and 11, 1947. The first of these resolutions reads as follows:
That a request be made to the Hon. H. F. G. Bridges, federal Minister of Fisheries, to appoint a superior officer of the United Fishermen of Quebec, a member of the national research office on fisheries, to represent the fishing industry of the province of Quebec.
In this connection I wish to mention that our industry in Quebec is not represented on the board. The second resolution reads as follows:

That a request be made to federal Department of Fisheries to assume entire responsibility of the fish inspection service in the province of Quebec as provided by the federal-provincial-agreement of 4922 and this in order to relieve a part of the provincial budget that could be used for other urgent needs of the industry.
This resolution is most important to our industry on the Gaspe coast. In that part of the country our fishermen cannot benefit from the many advantages of having dominion inspection, since this inspection is done by officials of the provincial government. I hope, now that our organized fishermen are asking to revert to dominion inspection that the autonomists of Quebec will not come out and say that this is an attack on the autonomy of the province, because those who are mainly interested in this dominion inspection and are asking for it are the fishermen of the province of Quebec themselves.
The third resolution reads as follows:
That the united fishermen of Quebec accept to actively collaborate with the International Bureau of Salt Fish to be organized in London, under the fallowing conditions:
(a)	No engagement shall be taken for a period of over one year;
(b)	the provincial department of fisheries shall pay a strong proportion of the contribution required from the producers of the province;
(c)	that Canada be represented on the executive office at London through the intermediary of a distinct section for the salt fish industry at the National Council of Fisheries but with the same secretary.
I do not think I need comment on that resolution. I know the minister has a copy of it and is giving it his active consideration.
Before closing my remarks, I wish again to impress on the government the urgent need for more suitable fishing harbours along the Gaspe coast.
On several occasions I have made representations, both in this house and out of it, to the departments concerned especially the Department of Public Works, on the urgent need for such harbours. I hope that our urgent plea will be heard this time and that action will soon be taken.
I think we must realize that the fishing industry of Canada is an important one. As I said at the beginning of these remarks I was informed a short time ago that we received favourable orders for fish from Italy. I am told that the shipments for which Italy is now asking are just sample shipments, but these orders will amount annually to some thirty million pounds of dried fish and some ten million pounds of frozen fish. These figures will, I believe, convince the committee that this industry is not to be neglected- and must be given every opportunity to increase its

Supply-Fisheries
production and should also be given all the advantages that the government has the power to give to our fishermen for the expansion of their industry.
As I intimated at the opening of my remarks, I have congratulations to offer to the minister on the efficient manner in which he is heading his department. I also wish to add my congratulations to his able assistant, the deputy minister of fisheries, who is new in the department but who is also doing a very good job indeed.

It is not my intention to make any extended address, but I should like to ask the minister one or two questions. Are any investigations being made at present with a view to conserving and increasing the salmon fisheries in the bay of Fundy? The Atlantic salmon is one of our best fish. The supply by n-o means meets the demand, I do Hot believe these fish are increasing in number; in fact I have reason to believe that they are decreasing. During the present season in the port of Saint John and along the shores of the bay of Fundy at Lorneville and at other fishing villages the catch is, I understand, very poor indeed, Study should be made to ascertain ways and means of conserving and increasing these fish in the bay of Fundy and also in other waters of the maritime provinces. It would help to conserve these fish if certain dams which serve no useful purpose at the present time were removed to permit the fish to get to their spawning bed. I have in mind dams at the mouth of the Mispec river in the county of Saint John, a great salmon river which enters the bay of Fundy about the village of St. Martin's. The Nashwaak river, as the minister knows, flows into the Saint John river almost opposite the city of Fredericton. On January 14, 1946, a delegation from the Saint John branch of the New Brunswick Fish and Game Protective Association interviewed the minister at the Admiral Beatty hotel in the city of Saint John. This delegation, which was headed by Gerald H. Cox, president of the association, asked for the construction of a new fishway on the Big Salmon river at St. Martin's in order that the river might be developed into a first-class salmon angling stream. The report that appeared in the papers stated:
. . . pointed out to the minister that the present fishway is not only poorly constructed but it is on the wrong side of the river, where the water is oftentimes too shallow for the fish to take advantage of this means of getting upstream.
The report goes on to say:
Mr. Cox stated that Mr. Bridges had promised to have the matter investigated, and it
was indicated that a survey would be made of the present fishway and conditions existing there.
What is the date of that?

I am reading a dispatch from the Telegraph-Journal of January 15, 1946. Has the survey been made? Has the investigation been completed and a report made to the minister's department? If an investigation has been completed and a report made, what action, if any, has been taken?
I read in the press not long ago that the minister was interviewed by a delegation from the city of Fredericton about the dam in the Nashwaak river. Has an investigation been held into the possibilities of improving the salmon fishing in that river? If a report has been made, what action, if any, is contemplated?
There is also a dam in the Mispec river near Saint John which the Saint John branch of the fish and game protective association has been endeavouring for a long time to have opened1 to enable the salmon to get upstream, but so far no arrangement has been entered into to permit that to be done. I should like to bring that dam, which obstructs the fish from getting up the river, to the minister's attention. There was another dam in the province of New Brunswick about which I should like to ask the minister a question and about which complaints have been made by some associations in Chipman or in Queens or Sunbury county. I refer to the dam at Newcastle near Newcastle bridge. Have the conditions of that dam been examined' with a view to having a fishway put in it to enable the fish to get up the stream? I should appreciate it if the minister will give us a statement as to the conditions at that place.
There are one or two other questions I should like to ask the minister. A year or two ago the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Fisheries issued an order preventing the sale of clams in certain areas along the shores of the bay of Fundy, in Saint John and in Charlotte county. I protested at the time. I had some correspondence with both departments about that order. I knew of no person who had suffered from eating these clams. I ate them regularly myself. However, the order was made. What steps are being taken to ascertain what causes the toxic condition in these clams? Has the biological branch of the minister's department or of any other department of government made a study of the matter for the purpose of ascertaining what causes the toxic condition? Certain areas which were closed have been opened at differ-
Supply-F isheries

ent times. This evening the minister kindly furnished me with a statement of the dates when certain areas which have been closed were opened, but certain areas are still closed. It has been a cause of great loss to the people who made a living digging these clams and selling them, and I think it is important for us to see that steps are taken, if they have not already been taken, to ascertain what has caused the toxic condition in these clams. So far as I know, there is no difference in these clams today, compared with what they were twenty or thirty years ago. However, if there is a difference, a thorough investigation should be made to findl out what causes that toxic condition.
There is one other matter to which I would refer. I would draw the minister's attention to these figures with regard to the lobster catch in the state of Maine. In 1939, 7,570,800 pounds of lobster were caught in the waters of Maine. In 1913, that had increased to 11,468,025 pounds. In 1944, there was a further increase to 13,300,000 pounds and, in 1945, another increase to 19,130,000 pounds. While the total catch of lobsters in Canada in 1939 was 31,466,000 pounds, in 1943 it was 30,000,000 pounds. It had dropped, and in 1944 it was
33,350,000	pounds. There had been a slight increase over a period of five years, but if you go back over a longer period of time you will find that there has been little variation in the figures. There has been no increase and, in some years, a decrease.
What I should like the minister to ask his officials is this. Will they explain why there has been such a large increase in the lobster catch in the state of Maine, a steady increase in the amount of lobsters caught in Maine, while in the whole of Canada, which is really the Atlantic coast, the lobster catch has remained stationary or has decreased?
Can it be said that the fact that in Maine they have established lobster hatcheries has nothing to do with the results shown by these figures? I should also like to ask the officials this question. If, as some of the officials state in their report, these lobster hatcheries do not produce results, why was it that only last year the state of Massachusetts, after, I presume, a most careful investigation, buiK a fish hatchery?
Was it a hatchery or a rearing pond?

I understand that it was a hatchery. As I read the dispatch, it was a hatchery. There must be some reason why the lobster fisheries along the Maine coast have increased. In six years they have more than doubled, while our lobster fisheries remain

stationary. There must be a reason for that. If it is not due to the hatcheries it must be due to something else, and we should discover why it is that our lobster fisheries remain stationary or only hold their own, while under the method they have adopted in Maine, their lobster fisheries have increased to such a great extent.
I will not delay the committee. There are one or two other matters I wish to speak about, but these are essential points I wanted to bring to the minister's attention, and I hope that in the course of his estimates he will give us as complete an answer as he can.

In contributing to this discussion I wish to thank the minister for the courteous way in which he meets the fishermen on the Pacific coast. It does [DOT] not go unnoticed by them, nor does the courtesy of his officials. It is not often that I rise to compliment a minister of the government, but in this case I believe it is his due.
I know I am taking my life in my hands in rising at this time because the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will be right on my heels. However I will do the best I can.
There are two points I would raise at this time. First, I would ask the minister to press upon the British Columbia government the need of a loan board for the fishermen. In the debate in the provincial legislature the Minister of Finance, Mr. Anscomb, turned it down on the ground that it would interfere with dominion-provincial relations. How this could possibly be so, I do not know, inasmuch as they have a loan board on the east coast. This is becoming absolutely necessary on the west coast because during the fishing season in area 2, many of the boats just made two trips. Some of the luckier ones made three, their boats are equipped to fish in area 2, and they are quite suitable for that purpose, but are not large enough to fish in area 3 continuously. If a loan board were established a greater proportion of the Canadian fleet would be enabled to compete in area 3. At the present time, to a large extent, it is a private hunting ground for Americans with their modern equipment.
I should like to see this loan board put through so that we could maintain our independently owned fleet on the Pacific coast, and this has particular reference of course to halibut. I should not like to see the fishing fleet fall back into large company-owned boats because these men do appreciate their freedom.
Another point I wish to bring up is the question of the fisheries prices support board. I should like to mention some of the fears that are bothering the men on the coast at the

present time. There is an embargo on the export of salmon, frozen and fresh. There is a premium price in the United States. The independently owned fleet sell their own fish through their own cooperative and are mainly interested in frozen and fresh fish, and they would like to enjoy that premium market which now exists in the United States.
It was pointed out to me that in certain cases on the east coast the fishermen of Gaspe are exporting their Gaspe salmon to the United States and enjoying that high price and at the same time eating British Columbia salmon.
Better food.

Yes. It may be better food, but let us not take it out on the west coast fishermen. In the past, certain laws have been put through that have been a detriment to west coast fishermen. First, during the war they had their income tax ten per cent deducted at the source. Dogfish livers also were up against the embargo, inasmuch as certain amounts were put into chicken feeds for Canadian use, whereas east coast cod livers had the right of the export market. We do not wish 'to see that condition arise owing to the setting up of this board, which is essentially a good piece of legislation; but it could be detrimental to the west coast fishermen, and they are rather sceptical of it in many cases, inasmuch as the prices support board will apply only to cod, which is a small item, taken in general, on the Pacific coast. So that in the condition in which we find ourselves in this country, being short of United States dollars, we could very well allow these fishermen to export their salmon and enjoy the premium price. At the same time it would bring in United States dollars to this country. I am sure that the members from British Columbia, such as the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, could enjoy eating goldeye or east coast cod.
Never.

They could sacrifice their ability to consume high quality fish in the meantime so that the fishermen could enjoy those high prices. I outline this programme to the minister because I have no doubt it will become a burning issue in the not far distant future.
Far be it from me to throw any rocks at the hon. member for Skeena. I want to congratulate him on what is probably the most reasonable speech I ever heard him make in the house.
Just one of the last twenty.

With
respect to Gaspe salmon enjoying the privilege of export to the United States, I wish to point out that it is comparable with our own spring salmon which we market fresh. I am sure the minister will tell him that if they w'ish this privilege, all they have to do is ask for a permit and they will receive it; and they can export all the spring salmon they have. There has been quite a high level of speeches in the house tonight. I am sure the minister has received some valuable suggestions. I, too, wish to congratulate him on the provision of this fund he was speaking of for relief purposes for European feeding. I do not want the committee to feel either that when the fish industry undertakes to deliver
88,000,000 worth of high-class fish products to the government, it is in any sense receiving a dole or subsidy. I think the government has looked around and has found no otheT source of high protein food available to it at the present time.
Good fish produce brains.
Yes.
That is the reason we all have them in British Columbia.

On the
setting up of the fisheries prices support board -and that, as I said, was a particularly good job-we are going to face a big problem. I should not like the board, or even members of parliament who are very often fond of talking the government out of money, ever to get the idea that this 825,000,000 is for the support of an industry which has not taken every means in its power to pull itself up by its own effort. We certainly do not want to use this money to create any surplus stocks of fish in this country. I just have the feeling that if certain fish is in surplus supply, the government should come to the conclusion that it would be an excellent plan for them to discontinue heavy fishing of that particular species.
It is getting late, and I sincerely trust that the minister will be able to get through with his estimates tonight; I will do everything I can to facilitate the progress. What I wished to place before the minister is the problem facing the pilchard industry on the west coast, in fish reduction, the making of meal and oil out of pilchards. That is the most hazardous business I know of in Canada. When I was first associated with it in 1926 there were twenty-six plants on the west coast, but through business failures and mortality in

the industry, they are now down to six operations. I might say that the industry is even more hazardous than the by-election, as far as I can see. It has always struck me that the fishing industry has never had from the government anything like the support the agricultural industry has had. Probably there are not enough members from the mari-times. I certainly do not begrudge the farmers any of the legislative measures they have been able to get through this house in order to support that great industry of theirs. However, as far as the pilchard industry is concerned, I feel that in the particular instance where the wartime prices and trade board has undertaken to place an embargo on the export of pilchard meal until we produce ten thousand tons-after that we are allowed to export fifty per cent-there is a measure of unfairness. I might point out that there is a difference in price of approximately $40 a ton in the United States, which is actually our traditional market, and the domestic price which we shall be able to receive. When you speak of ten thousand tons of pilchard meal- and I do not think the industry has any possibility this year of producing anything like that amount-it does seem to me that the minister-and 1 hesitate to advise him- ought to take a strong stand. When the wartime prices and trade board has undertaken to dictate to the fishing industry what they shall do in a matter of this kind, I feel that we are not being fairly treated. I would suggest to the minister that the industry be allowed to export fifty per cent of its production. I am quite sure that the Minister of Finance will support that measure because we would be able to get a large quantity of United States dollars in that way. I might also point out that if there is small production in the industry, that is certainly the time when we shall need higher prices; and, as the minister knows, there has been a substantial increase this year in the cost of production. I also think this is an appropriate time to call to the attention of the public generally in Canada that the production of fishmeal, rather than being a waste of a high-class fishery product, is actually an important contribution to our agricultural industry, because now we can produce far more beef and poultry by the mixtures of fishmeal with the ordinary grain feed.

Through this $8,000,000
which is being spent, is the fisherman to be guaranteed the present price for his fish? Is that indicated in the agreement or whatever there is when you buy? At the present time I understand that the fisherman gets about two cents a pound.
In the statement which I made the hon. member will note that in the purchase of $8 million worth of fish, prices will be paid which will be regarded as fair to the fishermen at this time.
Will the fishermen working in lake Athabaska, Great Slave lake and Great Bear lake profit by the arrangement the minister has announced?
What I am referring to there is this $8,000,000 of post-war UNRRA relief. Unfortunately that type of fish does not come from lake Athabaska or Great Slave lake.
Where are we getting it from?
It has to be of the salted or canned variety, and there is no salted or canned fish coming from lake Athabaska.

There has been quite a controversy across the country in regard to the use of luminous bait for fishing. I understand that comes under the minister's department. It is not provincial; it is federal. I just wondered if the minister had any remark to make with regard to that, because I know it has been taken up in all the provinces across the country, and they all disclaim any responsibility. They say it is purely federal.

In reply to the hon. member may I say I will look into the matter. This is the first time it has been brought to my attention by anyone.
Before the item carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer some of the questions that have been asked. Certainly I shall be very brief, because I am most anxious to get as many of these items through as possible. First, I wish to thank the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg for the constructive suggestions he has made. All I can say at the moment is that, of course, they will receive careful consideration. In connection with his remarks concerning the conservation of fisheries on the high seas I would point out that sometime in August a meeting of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations is to be held at Geneva, Switzerland, at which it is hoped that conservation regions will be established or at least considered.
In reply to the question by the hon. member for Queens I would say that the possible or probable break-down-it is really only an approximate break-down'-of the $8,000,000 he mentioned is as follows: on the east coast, dried and salted fish, 10,000.000 pounds amounting to approximately $1,800,000; pickled fish. 40.000 barrels amounting to approximately $520,000; bloaters, 50,000 boxes

53.320.000	for the east coast. On the west coast the possible order is for canned herring up to

The hon. member also asked for some comments regarding the existing lobster season on the Atlantic coast. I cannot give him any break-down or special information at the moment with regard to Prince Edward Island, since I did not anticipate that this question would be asked. The hon. member for Gaspe offered some remarks and referred especially to the fact that the Quebec united fishermen were not represented on the fisheries research board. If it were possible to give them representation on that board I should be only too happy to do so, but unfortunately at the present time all the positions on the board are filled. There are three representatives from the province of Quebec, but they happen to be scientists from McGill university, the university of Montreal, and Laval university. It does happen that, as far as Quebec is concerned, there is no representative on the board of the industry, either cooperative or what one might call private enterprise.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert asked quite a long series of questions. I am afraid I shall not be able to answer them all this evening. As far as Atlantic salmon are concerned, however, I would point out that investigations have been carried on in the bay of Fundy area for the past three years. If the hon.
member will refer to the annual report of the fisheries research board for 1946, he will see in it some reference to this matter.
In regard to reports and investigations made with respect to certain dams on certain rivers I would advise the hon. member that a report was made in respect of the dam on the Great Salmon river. That report is in the department, and I shall be only too happy to let him have it. In addition, an engineering investigation is being made to devise ways and means of improving the situation there.
As .to the investigations mentioned in the press concerning the Nashwaak river, I would advise the hon. member that the water in that river is still too high to permit those investigations to be carried on. I believe the water is still nine or ten feet above the ordinary summer level.
As to the dam at Newcastle Bridge, I am afraid that- is something I shall have to look into; at the moment I cannot seem to remember it.
Then I should like to point out with regard to the regulations concerning clams in the bay of Fundy area that all we do in this connection is impose <the prohibition on the digging of clams after we have been so advised by the Department of National Health and Welfare. A careful investigation is being madie by the St. Andrew's biological station of the fisheries research board in conjunction with the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and every effort is being made to find a solution to this most difficult and unfortunate problem in that area.
In regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena, I wish to thank the hon. member for his compliments as far as I am concerned. I would point out that this question of an embargo or export control on raw salmon in British Columbia, frozen and fresh, is not new this year, but is the continuation of a policy which has been in existence for some years. Not only is there an embargo on the export of the raw salmon; there is also an embargo on the export of canned salmon. It is quite possible that certain persons would like to obtain the benefit of the higher prices in the United States market, just as I have no doubt persons engaged in agriculture would like the benefit of higher United States prices, but there are similar regulations against the export of certain agricultural products as well. However I believe the export of red spring salmon to the United States market will not be too difficult, and I understand that permits will be freely issued by the representatives of the

Department of Trade and Commerce. It is .ntended to have the whole policy as flexible as possible.
I do not think there is any need of going into these matters in greater detail at the moment. To revert to the remarks of the hon. member for St. John-Albert concerning lobster hatcheries and lobster rearing ponds, I know a report was made on this matter, of which report I think I sent the hon. member a copy. It dealt with the advisability of reestablishing either or both hatcheries and rearing ponds, but our scientists have not come to the conclusion that they have been of the great benefit so many people think they are in Maine and Massachusetts. I am frank to admit that I am insisting that the matter be further studied, because of the arguments which have been advanced over the years, and because the fact that these hatcheries and rearing ponds have been maintained in those states undoubtedly indicates that they must have made some contribution to an increase in the take of lobsters in those areas. At any rate I assure the hon. member, as I would also assure the hon. member for Charlotte if he were here, that the matter is still being carefully considered.
